maintopic: REVISED SUBSIDY POLICY AFFECTING WESTERN DOMESTIC FIELD

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
maintopic: REVISED SUBSIDY POLICY AFFECTING WESTERN DOMESTIC FIELD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to make a statement on production subsidies on coal.
During the period of acute shortage of domestic coal in western Canada, subsidies were paid to certain high cost producers of coal, to stimulate production. The subsidies paid covered all losses, plus an item of profit, and were justified as a basis of assistance when coal had to be obtained at any reasonable cost, but left no incentive on the part of the operator to reduce his cost to a minimum.
The situation in western Canada has now completely changed. Domestic coal is in surplus supply and it has been necessary for the government to consider a more equitable method of assisting those mines that might collapse if all government assistance were withdrawn. On the recommendation of the emergency coal production board, the following revised subsidy policy affecting the western domestic field has been adopted:
Effective April 1, 1944, coal mine operators who have been operating at'a loss will be paid a maximum subsidy as follows:
Sixty-five cents per net ton for mines operating in the Edmonton area.
Thirty cents per net ton for mines operating in the Drumheller area.
Thirty cents per net ton for mines operating in the Camrose area.
Thirty-five cents per net -ton for mines operating in the Lethbridge area.
Thirty-five cents per net ton on shaft mines in the Coalspur area.
Thirty-five cents per net ton for mines operating in the Saunders area.
Fifteen cents per net ton on shaft mines operating in the Saskatchewan field.
The above subsidies represent the average increased cost incurred by operators in the various fields due to wage increases and the cost-of-living bonus.
In cases where the operator has been able to absorb part of the increase in cost, an alternative subsidy of a flat rate per ton equivalent

Coal

to the average subsidy approved during the months of October, November, and December, 1943, plus cost-of-living bonus, will be paid, provided such bonus is not greater than the maximum subsidy per ton named above for the various fields.
The revised subsidy will be paid for the government fiscal year 1944-45, but subject to review at the end of each three months.
Subsidy may be reduced if the review shows that a profit greater than the company's standard profits is earned.
The foregoing is an attempt to meet the present situation of coal production in western Canada. It is recognized that the war has had the effect of changing and disturbing prewar arrangements for the production and marketing of coal in all parts of Canada. It seems probable that the dominion coal policy will require revision as it will apply to post-war years.
Therefore, the government will appoint a royal commission, charged with the duty of studying all .aspects of the production and distribution of coal in Canada, to report to the government with recommendations for such alterations of the pre-war coal policy as its findings may indicate as necessary or desirable.

subtopic: SUSPENSION OP SPECIAL ORDER WITH RESPECT TO SITTING OP WEDNESDAY NEXT
speechtext:
I should like to say a word

to the house about the proceedings of the present week. As the house will be adjourning on Friday for the Easter vacation, I think it would probably suit the convenience of members generally if instead of sitting on Friday night we were to sit on Wednesday afternoon. If that is agreeable, I would move:
That the resolution passed by the house on February 21 last with respect to Wednesday sittings be suspended in relation to Wednesday next.
On Friday night it was announced that this afternoon we would continue with the munitions and supply items under the war appropriation resolution and this evening take up some minor bills. I feel, however, that we should, before adjourning for Easter, make as much headway as possible with the war appropriation measure. The government therefore would prefer to continue this evening with the discussion of the war appropriation estimates on munitions and supply, and if they are not concluded to-night continue with those estimates to-morrow; the only exception being that in the last part of the evening, between half past ten and eleven, we would seek again to get an item or two into supply.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: SUSPENSION OP SPECIAL ORDER WITH RESPECT TO SITTING OP WEDNESDAY NEXT
speechtext:
I think it is wise to go as far as we can in expediting the war appropriation resolution debate, and I simply want to say this to the Prime Minister. I should like very much if the government, during the Easter recess, would consider the advisability of restoring Wednesday afternoon sittings.
I do not bring this up in any desire to quarrel with the government over this matter; I did so once before, and I think perhaps one quarrel is enough. In my opinion, however, members generally have found that the suspension of the Wednesday afternoon sittings has not worked out in the best interests of parliament, although I must confess that the argument which the Prime Minister put on record before, from the point of view of the work of the war committee of the cabinet, is one which of course should also have serious consideration. I am prepared to give that consideration to the right hon. gentleman and his cabinet.
The fact is, however, that from the point of view of committee work, I have checked the work that has been done by the committees, and I find that of the standing committees, up to date, only three out of fifteen have met at all and only one of these met for part of one Wednesday. The situation with regard to the other special committees is that the majority of them have met on Wednesdays, but very few of them have worked on either Monday or Friday and very few on Tuesdays. That means, as I think most members will agree, that we have not been utilizing Wednesday afternoons in the manner anticipated by the government.
I suggest to the Prime Minister that there must surely be some way by which the cabinet's work can be arranged to provide that neither the members of the war committee nor the Prime Minister need be in the house on Wednesday afternoon. We would be prepared to facilitate that arrangement as far as possible, and perhaps some of the cabinet ministers whose work is possibly not so important, or at any rate so heavy, could be utilized for that purpose, so that we might have Wednesday afternoon for ordinary house work.
We have felt that it retarded the work of the session to have Wednesday taken out of the week, and that has been borne out by the experience we have had in the last few weeks during which the new practice has prevailed. I would ask the Prime Minister to give serious consideration to the suggestion, because with the tremendously heavy agenda I think it would be of great help in getting the work under way and the business of the house coming up in proper sequence.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SUSPENSION OP SPECIAL ORDER WITH RESPECT TO SITTING OP WEDNESDAY NEXT
speechtext:
That may be perfectly true, but my hon. friend has not the responsibility that those of us who are members of the government have. It is quite easy' to say that the opposition can get along without the ministers of the crown, particularly those belonging to the war committee of the cabinet, but I would remind my hon. friend that there are very few questions that come up this session that do not in one way or another touch some aspect of the war, and I have grave doubts as to the wisdom of all members of the war committee of the cabinet being wholly absent from the house at any time. However, do not let my hon. friend imagine that Wednesdays are reserved simply for meetings of the war committee of the cabinet. There are meetings of the entire
Wednesday Sittings

cabinet as well that have to be held, and have been held on Wednesdays, as well as the meetings of the war committee of the cabinet. It is a little difficult to have hon. members realize that at a time of war, and particularly at this stage of the war, there is a tremendous amount of business which can be done only by the executive, and which has to be done only by the executive in comparison with what is the case at any other time.
I mention the present stage of the war. The cabinet to-day is giving almost as much consideration to matters that pertain to post-war affairs as it is giving to matters actually related to the war itself. In the very nature of things many of these matters cannot be disclosed because they involve a careful consideration of what is being proposed by other countries as well as by Canada. We receive from time to time, almost daily in fact, communications which set forth representations on different matters that come to us, some from the government of the United Kingdom, some from the United States, some from the other dominions, on such all-important questions as those related to what will come up immediately after the war is over, or when there is an armistice. These post-war problems have to be considered. They are very important. If a mistake is made in a matter of policy on something that affects the whole future of the relations between nations, it is a very serious mistake indeed. I am not assuming that we are going to make mistakes, but we certainly wish to avoid them and so far as Canada is concerned to give our mature judgment to these questions and to give as wise decisions as it is possible to give.
I do say that it is not humanly possible for members of the cabinet to deal, with a full sense of responsibility, with the class of questions we have now before us and also attend in this House of Commons on Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, Friday afternoon and night and Wednesday afternoon. That is just not possible, and I think it better to speak plainly in this way in order that the matter may be definitely understood. I am perfectly sure that in the United Kingdom, for example, they have much more business to transact than we have, and that parliament there is as anxious as we are to sit and get through its business as rapidly as possible, but they have found it necesary, notwithstanding that they do not sit in the evenings at all, to cut down the normal sittings of the House of Commons and reduce them very considerably. It is for the reason that the subjects that have to be considered are so involved, yet so important, and the implications arising out of them so vast, that they do require more than ordinary consideration.

I need not say to my hon. friend that one cannot leave everything to Saturday and Sunday. Human endurance does reach its limits. I believe every minister is working most of seven days as it is, but the fact that he may not be obliged to work at high pressure every day of the week does make a little difference. Let me say to my hon. friend that the government will consider what he has suggested and do what we have done, for example, this afternoon-arrange for a Wednesday sitting where it seems desirable to have it. But I do not wish to make any promise as to any change in the procedure at as early a stage in the session as this.

subtopic: POSTPONEMENT UNTIL AUGUST 31 OP FINAL PAYMENT ON 1943 INCOME

speakeroldname: Hon. C. W. G. GIBSON (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: POSTPONEMENT UNTIL AUGUST 31 OP FINAL PAYMENT ON 1943 INCOME
speechtext:
I desire to make a statement concerning the payment of 1943 income tax. Owing to an unusual combination of circumstances, which is not likely to occur again, the government has decided to postpone the payment of any balance of unpaid income tax falling due on the 30th of April, from that date to the 31st of August, without interest.
Taxpayers are advised that this announcement is in respect of the payment of the balance of taxes falling due on the 30th of April, and does not refer to the time of filing income tax returns. Income tax returns must still be filed on or before the 30th of April.
It will be observed that this announcement falls into two parts-one, postponing the time of payment to the 31st of August, and the other confirming that the filing of returns must be made by the 30th of April as required by law.
Perhaps a comment on the postponed payment should be made. It remains open for any individual to make payment of the unpaid balance of 1943 tax falling due on the 30th of April at any time between now and the 31st of August without any interest being added. After the 31st of August interest at five per cent, as provided by law, will become payable.
The income tax returns, as the law at present requires, must be filed on the 30th of April. The reason for requiring these returns to be filed on the present due date is to enable the income tax division to proceed with the assessing of returns, to avoid delay in making
refunds and the issuing of compulsory saving certificates.

Postponed conscientious objectors, other than those directed to alternative service work camps for employment, may be required to enter into an arrangement whereby a portion of their earnings is deposited in a chartered bank by their employers to the credit of the Canadian Red Cross Society. No alternative service worker, unless he be self-employed, undertakes to deposit any amount directly to the credit of the Canadian Red Cross Society. The arrangement regarding employment is that the earnings of the alternative service worker shall be at the rate of the going wages for the work done. From the earnings certain statutory wages, living allowances and deductions are made and, at the discretion of the alternative service officer, dependents' allowances may be granted. The amount the Canadian Red Cross Society receives is that balance which the employer undertakes to deposit at a chartered bank after a district treasury officer has certified that the earnings and deductions are proper and in accordance with the agreement.

Mr. Speaker, I am informed that there have been forwarded ito my office a large number of resolutions on the subject referred to. The resolutions are similarly worded. It is perfectly evident some one or more persons have been circulating communications with a view to having them forwarded to my office. The question is of the kind which, were it to be answered literally, might convey a wholly erroneous impression. For example, I might say I have received thousands of communications identically worded concerning some things-the postage being free. Were I asked to recall how many of these had been received, and were to say that thousands had come in, such an answer would be wholly misleading. For the most part they would represent the opinions of a mere handful of persons. There have not been thousands in this case, but an answer as to the number that have come in would be misleading the public as to the significance of the reply given. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think at the outset in answering my hon. friend's question I should make it clear that Canada has gone very far in restricting the rights of landlords to get possession of their own property, possibly farther than any other united nation. Six months' notice is now the general rule, eviction being impossible during the winter months. Owners may obtain possession only for their own use or for their immediate family. In multiple family dwellings, tenure is even more secure, an owner being unable to get. possession unless he is now living in rented accommodation
elsewhere or is living in a single dwelling, and then he may obtain possession only for his personal use.
In greater Montreal, which is the area to which my hon. friend referred in his question, the leasehold regulations of the wartime prices and trade board have had the effect of giving security of tenure to a very high proportion of tenants. It is estimated that 86 per cent of the population, or 220,000 families, live in multiple family dwellings in the Montreal area. I might point out that in normal times, something like 50,000 of these flats change hands on May 1 in each year. Last year, largely as a result of the regulations, this large movement was reduced to about 12,000, and this year, by reason of the order relating to multiple family dwellings to which I have already referred, eviction notices have been received by only 1,258 tenants in multiple family dwellings.
In spite of all that has been done, it is regrettably true that there will be cases of individual hardship. This seems unavoidable when people are shifting about in great numbers and labour and materials are in short supply. Moreover, the imposition of further restrictions would not eliminate hardship. Indeed, it is certain that further restrictions, such as, for example, the freezing of all leases, which has been suggested, would create new hardships though perhaps for different individuals. Many owners have acted in good faith on the strength of the present regulations and have made arrangements to vacate their present accommodation in the expectation of being able to get possession of their own homes on May 1 next. The house will realize that each of these transactions is a link in a chain of other arrangements which would be disturbed by further changes in the regulations.
It is inevitable that under -conditions of wartime congestion a certain number of citizens of Montreal, as well as elsewhere, may find it necessary to make temporary or emergency arrangements for accommodation. On the whole, however, by the various regulations to which I have referred the scope of the problems has been reduced until it is now in reality a local condition which concerns a comparatively limited number of citizens. The wartime prices and trade board has had the situation under review at all times and has come to the conclusion that it would be inadvisable at this time to impose further restrictions on owners of property in order to meet local conditions. After care-
Clark Ruse Aircraft

ful consideration and consultation with the board, the government agrees with the board's decision.
The house will appreciate that in the restrictive orders already in effect, the dominion government has gone far in interfering with ordinary rights as between owner and tenant, which, except for wartime emergency powers, would be beyond its constitutional authority.
A delegation representing a group of Montreal tenants was in Ottawa last week and submitted certain recommendations, and the Acting Minister of Finance has to-day written to the head of this delegation along the lines which I have indicated in answering my hon. friend's question.

On March 16 the Department of Munitions and Supply notified the Department of Labour that approximately 500 men would be laid off beginning March 20. Arrangements immediately were made to deal with the situation. Men who have been postponed from military service and do not have special skills will be called up for the army.
A survey already has been completed in this connection. As a result it has been ascertained that 111 men will be called for army service, of whom it is anticipated most will be acceptable. Postponement of 18 will be continued because they have special skills, and 109 others are in designated age groups but are not acceptable for army service on medical grounds. The lunch room at the plant has been taken over by the manager of the Halifax national selective service office and 15 of his staff, and they are interviewing those laid off and placing them in other jobs. I stated that approximately 111 will be called to the army. This leaves 75 who are in the process of being placed. The manager of our Halifax office anticipates no difficulty in placing men almost as quickly as they are laid off.

I should like to revert to the question of synthetic rubber, particularly the set-up of the plant of Polymer Corporation at Sarnia. This is a matter in which there is considerable public interest and concerning which a great deal of information has been made available. Last year we had quite a discussion on it in the house, during which the Minister of Munitions and Supply spoke on Wednesday, June 16. Also last year a number of sessional papers were tabled which provided information on the subject. I refer in particular to sessional papers Nos. 388 and 303A. A number of orders in council respecting this plant have been tabled. There were four in 1942-P.C. 2369, P.C. 3177, P.C. 4252, and P.C. 10008, and there was also P.C. 2799 of April 8, 1943.
In addition to the information which has been brought down in the house, a great deal of publicity has been given the Polymer
1S6S

plant by the press and by magazines. On Thursday, March 23, the matter was discussed again in this chamber and the minister contributed to the debate.
I believe the people of Canada as they get to know some of the facts of the situation will share the pride which the minister has in the Polymer plant. I enjoy the pride which the Minister of Munitions and Supply expresses from time to time in government owned projects. He is sometimes referred to, both by his friends and by his enemies, as the Tory of the present government; yet I know of no one who expresses greater pride in certain projects that are publicly owned. Take for example his attitude towards Trans-Canada Air Lines, which we all share, and his attitude towards the fact that this Polymer plant is owned by the Canadian people.
There is reason for that pride, first of all in the fact that the plant has been completed in rather a short time, considering the difficulties of construction in war time. There is also the fact that the Canadian people, through their government, have found a way to build a plant that will operate on a brand new process. This was not something that could simply be copied; a real pioneering job had to be done. We can also be proud of the fact that when the country was faced with dwindling supplies of rubber it was possible to get this plant into operation speedily enough to make up for the shortages of crude rubber.
I would add my congratulations to those already expressed to the engineers and technicians who designed this thoroughly integrated plant, and brought it into production in such a short time. Through the medium of this plant we have been able to make this very vital contribution to the war effort. Nevertheless I have certain misgivings for the future growing out of the set-up of the plant at Sarnia. I would call the attention of the minister and the committee to these circumstances. Before expressing any misgivings, however, I have tried to convey my feelings of pride, and to voice my commendation with regard to the building of the plant, in the hope that there will be no misunderstanding on that point.
My misgivings relate principally to the post-war period and in particular to the setup of the plant in so far as it is being operated by private firms brought in by the government for this work. Publicity has been given to the fact that the plant is being operated in this way by the terms of order in council P.C. 2799 of April 8, 1943, and also

by the remarks which the minister has made in the house. When I express my misgivings as to what is going to happen in the post-war period I want to make it clear that these misgivings are not those of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). If I understood him correctly, the member for Lake Centre on Thursday of last week, and also in the remarks he made last year, was afraid that in the post-war period it would be against the interests of private enterprise for this plant to be continued as a government-owned project.
If I may say so, I feel that the hon. member does not fully understand the set-up. I cannot see that it is one that is in any way against the interests of private enterprise in the post-war period. On the contrary, my fear is that the set-up we have at the presenttime, if it is continued into the post-war period, is one that will result in the benefit of this government-financed, government-owned project accruing principally to private enterprise. I shall have something to say as I go along with regard to that set-up, as I see it from a study of the documents to which I have referred, and I should be glad if, some time during the debate, the member for Lake Centre would make clear what it is he would like to have done with the plant to make it more beneficial to private enterprise than it will be as it is now arranged.
As I have said, my fear with regard to the post-war period is that the benefit of the plant, in spite of the fact that it has been financed with public funds and is owned by the people, will accrue to private enterprise. The set-up, as the documents indicate, and as the minister has outlined, involves government ownership of the company known as Polymer Corporation Limited. The company to which I have referred has built the plant with government funds. The amount of money is between $45,000,000 and $50,000,000. The government took all the risks in connection with building of the plant in a field in which it was not possible to copy other plants in operation.
My own feeling about it is that the cost of construction has probably been kept down as well as it could under the circumstances. It is inevitable that the building of the first plant of this kind would cost more than the building of any subsequent plant. If there is any such greater cost in connection with the building of the first plant, the govern-

ment, on behalf of the people, has incurred this greater cost and in that sense has taken the risks of pioneering.
The total cost of the plant is being paid for out of the war appropriation. I do not find anywhere the suggestion that it is to be paid back out of some kind of depreciation later on. It is simply a charge against the war appropriation bill. Having built the plant with public funds and having taken all these risks, the government has then to consider the problem of operating it and producing synthetic rubber, the product for which it was set up. According to the order in council to which I have already referred, P.C. 2799 of April 8, 1943, the plant is being operated by three companies. First of all there is the St. Clair Processing Corporation. I understand that this company operates that part of the plant where butadiene is made from petroleum and also looks after miscellaneous services around the property. Secondly, there is the Dow Chemical Company of Canada Limited, which looks after that part of the plant which produces styrene from petroleum. The third company involved is the Canadian Synthetic Rubber Company, Limited, which, as the minister said the other day, operates the polymerization plant where the two principal elements, butadiene and styrene, are combined into buna-S rubber.
As hon. members know, these three companies, although they are incorporated specifically for the purposes I have indicated, namely, the operation of sections of the Polymer Corporation plant at Sarnia, are subsidiaries of other companies. The St. Clair Processing Corporation is a subsidiary of Imperial Oil Limited. Dow Chemical Company of Canada Limited is a subsidiary of the Dow Chemical Company of the United States, and Canadian Synthetic Rubber Company is a subsidiary owned by four Canadian rubber companies, sometimes referred to as the Big Four in the rubber industry'-Goodyear, Goodrich, Firestone and the Dominion Rubber Company. It is these private corporations that have been called in to operate this government-financed and government-owned plant.
I should like to make a point here about our atittude towards this procedure. It is perfectly clear that the men connected with these private companies are the men who have had the experience and some knowledge of the processes involved. They were the men who should be called in to do this work. That is particularly true at a time such as this when we are calling on all our people to devote whatever abilities they may have to the tasks that must be performed in connection with the war. We are calling upon thousands of our young men to give of their services in the
armed forces and in many cases to give their lives. It is only right and proper, therefore, that the men with the ability and the experience in the lines related to the production of synthetic rubber should be called in to do that particular job. The government would have been remiss had it not called them in. Let that be perfectly clear, so far as our attitude is concerned.
But, Mr. Chairman, here is where1 our viewpoint differs. We feel that the calling in of these men to give of their brains and ability and experience where they could most usefully contribute to the national service should not mean that the corporations with which they are connected should in the period of the war, or in the post-war period, be given any special privileges or special advantages as a result of the war-time necessities of the situation. Yet it is my contention that that is exactly what will happen under the present set-up if it is continued over into the postwar period. Let us look at the situation as it arises out of the procedure which has been followed.
Petroleum is the principal raw material that goes into the production of synthetic rubber at Sarnia. The petroleum from which the gases are taken off for the manufacture of butadiene and styrene comes from Imperial Oil Company, and a subsidiary of the Imperial Oil Company known as the St. Clair Processing Corporation has been called in to operate the part of the plant which does this work. In other words, a private corporation with a particular interest in petroleum is right in there operating that part of the plant.
Similarly, chemicals go into the manufacture of synthetic rubber to a considerable extent. The Dow Chemical Company, through its subsidiary, Dow Chemical Company of Canada Limited, is in there operating that part of the plant where chemicals are most deeply involved. They are naturally interested in chemicals that are used in the production of synthetic rubber, and they are also interested in the new processes by means of which different chemicals can be taken off from petroleum. In other words they are interested in the scientific developments which will be taking place right along as the production of synthetic rubber continues, and, as the minister himself said on Thursday of last week, that is one of the interesting and important phases in the manufacture of synthetic rubber at Sarnia. But what we have done is to put a private corporation with a particular interest in chemicals right inside operating the chemical end of the plant.
Then there is the Canadian Synthetic Rubber Company, which, as the minister has pointed out, is wholly owned by four Canadian rubber
War Appropriation-Supplies

companies. The main purpose of the plant is the production of synthetic rubber, and making that rubber available to rubber manufacturing companies so that they can produce the materials that are necessary in time of war. But when the war is over these same private rubber companies will continue to be interested in the availablility of synthetic rubber for the production of tires and rubber goods of all kinds. In other words, they have a special and a very particular interest in the production of synthetic rubber. They will also have an interest in the quality of that rubber, whether it is kept as high as possible so that tires will last a long time, or whether the grade should be kept down a little so that the consumers will have to buy more tires as time goes on. My point is that in the post-war period the private firms that have the greatest interest in what will be going on at the Sarnia plant, both at the end where the raw materials are taken in and at the other end where the final product is turned out, are right there now doing the operating.
I say again that the government would have been remiss had it not called in the people with the ability to do this sort of job. That does not mean, however, that at the expense of the public you should give special privileges to the corporations behind these men and to the financial interests behind those corporations. I do not relish the idea of attacking individuals in connection with a matter of this kind; yet I think it should be pointed out that along with the taking into the plant of the men who were equipped to do this work, we find that men of high standing in the rubber industry have been called in and placed in positions of high authority. For example, the general manager of the Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company is president of the Polymer Corporation. I find also that the vice-president of the Dominion Rubber Company is the deputy rubber controller in the Department of Munitions and Supply. I have met both these gentlemen, as I have met others in similar positions. They are fine gentlemen; they know their business, and I have nothing against them personally. What does get under my skin, however, is that because their abilities are needed in time of war we put ourselves in the position that we give special profit and special privilege to the corporations behind them, and to the power of finance behind those corporations. These men are interested, as we all are, in the best possible prosecution of the war effort; but also, inevitably, they are interested in +he welfare and profits of the companies on whose payrolls they remain, and with which presumably they will continue to be associated

in the post-war period. It is these men who are in a position to operate this synthetic rubber plant at Sarnia, if they so desire, in such a manner as to make the best possible use of the raw materials that come in at one end, and at the other end to make synthetic rubber available to private rubber companies on terms which will be to the greatest possible advantage of those rubber companies.
If I may elaborate what I said a moment ago in referring to the hon. member for Lake Centre, surely this should make it clear that the set-up is not in any way inimical to the interests of private enterprise; on the contrary it will be of great advantage to them. When people give the benefit of their brains, their ability and their experience, they should receive all praise and full reward; but beyond that, the benefit which accrues from the application of brains, ability and experience in a plant like this, financed by public funds, should go not to private corporations, privately financed, but to the people as a whole.
In time of war, we find ourselves in this position, that at times we have to disregard cost 'and see to it that the materials necessary for the war are produced. To that extent the benefit of this procedure in connection with Polymer accrues to the people as a whole; for we are getting materials of war for our common defence. I want to see that the benefit of this new scientific development, this new project at Sarnia, will continue to accrue to the people of Canada as a whole after the war is over.
Let me repeat the picture as I see it in the post-war period. We shall find that we have at Sarnia a modern synthetic rubber plant, as the minister has said, integrated to a greater extent than any other synthetic rubber plant in North America. I think the minister's invitation to hon. members to visit that plant should be accepted by all who can possibly do so, so that we may share the pride of the minister in the fact that this is our plant, that it belongs to the people,of Canada. But in spite of the fact that it will be our plant this product will be available in the first instance to the private rubber manufacturers; and before it gets to the Canadian people for civilian use in the post-war period it will go through not only the manufacturing but also the economic processes of a private enterprise system, so that the first benefit of this new plant will accrue to these, private corporations and to the financial interests behind them. My desire is that the total benefit of this new idea, the plant having been financed by the people of Canada, should accrue to the Cana-

War Appropriation-Supplies
dian people as a whole, making allowance for a just reward to the engineers, technicians and workmen who built the plant.
We should take note of the fact that we have paid for this plant in full out of the money provided in the war appropriations. By contrast-perhaps, as a matter of fact, it is not by contrast; perhaps it is the same story in the long run-when the Aluminum Company of Canada, a private corporation, needed to expand its facilities for war-time production, the government decided that it should be given special depreciation so that it could take care of the total cost of that plant during the period of the war. I need not go into that argument again, but we have pointed out that in our view this means that after the war that private company will have increased facilities and increased productive capacity that have been paid for by the people. There is no suggestion of depreciation as far as this government-owned plant is concerned; the argument is that the government owns it anyway, so why depreciate it. I point out, however, that the net result is the same. You allow depreciation in the one instance, which means that the people pay for the plant though it is still in private hands. In the other instance you do not allow depreciation because the people are paying for the plant anyway.

May I ask my hon. friend
what people paid for the aluminum plant?

The people of the
united nations.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I do not know that we
want to go into that debate again, but our point in that connection has been that when the price for aluminum was set, it was set at a figure high enough to include depreciation allowances which would take care of the cost of the plant during the three, four or five years of the war. I believe that at the end of 1945 the aluminum plant extensions will be fully paid for. The point I make now is that while one method is followed in one case, that of special depreciation, the method of government ownership without special depreciation is followed in the other, and the net result is the same. At the end of the war both plants are fully paid for. The aluminum company plant is owned by a private corporation, and the Polymer Corporation plant, although owned by the people, is being operated by these private concerns, using their raw materials and turning out products for their use.
There is another way in which it seems to me the government is strengthening the-control of private interests in the rubber industry, as a result of, shall I say war-time necessity. Let me make it clear to the
minister that when Jhe came up against the problem of the cutting off of the supply of crude rubber, after Pearl Harbor, 'he faced the necessity of getting the synthetic plant built and into operation. He called in the people who_ could help him in that job, and we have no' complaint about that. Our contention is, however, that he, the house and country should look at the results of that procedure, so far as the post-war period is concerned. Along with the government money which has gone into the building of the Polymer plant we have also had the expenditure of a considerable sum of government money to enlarge the plants of rubber manufacturing companies.
In the last two or three days we have had circulated among us a little booklet containing a report on the government financed expansion of industrial capacity in Canada as at December 31, 1943. Quotations have been made from it by a number of hon. members. I have gone through it looking for those amounts of money made available by way of capital assistance to private rubber companies. I understand there are fifty or sixty rubber companies manufacturing rubber goods in Canada. Naturally, when there are that many of them a few will be large and many will be small. I have gone through this report to find out what assistance is being given to private rubber companies, and I find that although there are fifty or sixty of those companies manufacturing rubber goods in Canada, the names of only eight such companies appear in this report.
Let me make it clear that I d'o not know the kind of work in which every company listed in the booklet is engaged. Some hon. members may be able to point out that some companies, the names of which do not so indicate, are rubber manufacturing companies. However I have been, able to find only eight. The total amount of capital assistance made available to those eight is, according to this report, $4,861,699. First of all there are the Big Four, the owners of The Canadian Synthetic Rubber Company Limited. I refer to Goodyear, Goodrich, Firestone and Dominion. The other four are Dunlop, Seiberling,. Gutta Percha and Miner. Of that $4,861,699 made available to only eight out of sixty rubber companies in Canada, $3,900,179, or 80 per cent, is made available to the Big Four. If we add in one more, namely Dunlop, and make it the Big Five, we find that they received 86 per cent of the total made available to these companies.
I know the argument is that these were the big companies, and that they were the
War Appropriation-Supplies

ones that could expand their plants and take on additional orders for the war effort. I shall not take time to deal with it in detail, but I have before me a most interesting sessional paper, No. 139, tabled Friday, January 28, 1944, which sets out the figures respecting contracts let by the 'Department of Munitions and Supply to firms from which it has taken in dollar-a-year men. I find in there some figures as to the size of contracts given to some of the companies I have named as being among the Big Four.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order; the hon. member has spoken forty minutes.

Last week I asked the Minister of Munitions and Supply whether it would be possible to give us an estimate as to the cost of aircraft. I see that he has produced what appears to be a most excellent graph, showing the ratio between man-hours per pound of airframe produced, and the cumulative aircraft delivered. Would it be possible for him to give that statement to the committee this afternoon?

Hon. members are aware that I have always objected to giving costs in the House of Commons, and I believe it might be well at this time to state my reason for so objecting. The graph I have asked to have distributed to members shows the man-hour performance curve,, of good performance, and used to check the performance of our plants. The elements of cost in an aircraft are, largely, material and labour, the latter being translated into the number of men multiplied by the number of hours they work, expressed by the term man-hours. Materials are fairly constant. It does not matter whether we produce one aircraft, or one hundred, or five thousand; generally speaking material costs are not a variable factor. Aluminum costs the same, and other materials cost about the same.
I would point out, however, that the productions of planes, per man working one hour, changes very rapidly as production continues. If my hon. freind will look at the top curve, he will find that it is a curve showing good performance for a plant making fifteen aircraft a month, while the lower curve is the good-performance curve for a plant making 150 aircraft a month. We have other curves fitting the particular situation we find in any of our plants. If hon. members will look at the bottom curve, showing good performance for 150 aircraft a month, they will see that the cost of man-hours in the one-hundredth aircraft is just about twice the cost of manhours used in producing the one-thousandth aircraft. And the cost of man-hours used in

producing the two-thousandth aircraft is lower still. The contrast is even sharper on the curve above, which applies for smaller production.
My hon. friend may ask me, as he did, as to the cost of producing an aircraft at Victory Aircraft plant. As he will see that cost depends on the particular aircraft that he may select. Each aircraft produced costs less than the preceding one, and that goes on for a considerable time. After the two-hundredth aircraft the man-hour curve begins to level off, and the difference will be less. Therefore it is very unfair to compare performance at one plant, with performance at another, by comparing the cost of current output at each plant. We must know the background; we must know how many units have been produced by one plant, against the number that have been produced by another. We must know the rate of production at one plant as compared with the rate of production at another. I might say that the man-hour factor illustrated on the graph is not confined to aircraft production ; it applies .pretty well to any sort of production that is repetitive in character. It would apply to ships-there is the same progressive reduction in man-hours for the production of ships. The curve also explains why, in ordinary times, we pay more for automobiles in Canada than is paid in the United States. Their production lines are dealing with vastly larger quantities and their man-hour costs per unit usually are much lower than can be obtained with the limited output of our own production lines.
Therefore I hope hon. members will not ask me for the costs per unit of output at our various plants. It would be wholly unfair to give them. Plotted here on this graph are several curves of our own actual performance. I may say that these are kept up to date in our office, and comparisons are made with the curve of good performance. This curve of good performance is used all over this continent for aeroplane mass production work. I may say that our production in terms of man-hours, is very good indeed. Generally speaking, our actual performance is better than the curve of good performance.
Better than?

Better than the curve which has been agreed upon as the curve of good performance. Usually we are below that curve. My hon. friend will see that curve F is the longest of the lot, and he will see at one stage that there is quite a jump in the curve. These jumps are caused by major modifications, or substantial changes in the aircraft,

War Appropriation-Supplies
which slowed down the rate of output, and temporarily shot up the man-hours per plane. My hon. friend will see that our performance curves follow fairly well the standard curves of good performance. Generally speaking, our costs are very satisfactory when measured with performance and costs in the United States or in the United Kingdom.
Could the minister give the formula for working out these curves?
I cannot.
It is empirical?

It is empirical. The plants which are known to be good performers are taken. A study of the industry was made in order to see what should be expected from established plants when bringing new types of aircraft into production.

I thought the committee would be interested in getting some idea of whether we could continue to have an aircraft industry in Canada after the war is over. I think it is important that steps should be taken now in order that the aircraft industry may be perpetuated in Canada. The information that we now have may give a lead as to the possibility of that happening. I understand that the commercial type of aircraft to be produced is the DC-4, which is approximately a 40-place job for commercial transportation. These figures give us some idea of what it is going to mean to the country to maintain an aircraft industry.
An old quarrel between the minister and myself is in connection with the production of aircraft engines. As yet no aircraft engines have been produced in Canada. Do the costs of producing aircraft engines follow these curves if produced elsewhere? In other words, are we now buying Allison engines or Rolls Royce Merlin engines or Packard engines cheaper to-day than we were eighteen months ago? If so, our engine costs must have been reduced very considerably.
I agree with the minister when he says that it is unfair to make comparisons between costs, particularly in connection with experimental types of aircraft. I imagine that a year ago the cost of producing the first two or three Mosquitos was a fabulous sum, and I realize that it would be unfair to compare present costs. But I realize also that we must have some idea of our ability to produce aircraft in competition with other united nations. That is why I asked this question. Is the minister going to place this information on Hansard?

I shall be glad to ask that the graph be placed on Hansard, if I can get unanimous consent.
(The graph referred to-aircraft man-hour performance curves-was published separately.)

A week or so ago I had an opportunity of visiting once more the Victory and de Havilland plants. This was the first visit I had made in about nine or ten months, and I must say that the conditions in both plants seemed to have improved materially over what they were when I was last there. There are some questions I should like to ask in connection with aircraft production and arising out of the questions asked by the hon. member for York West. The minister has indicated that his opinion is that the performance record in Canada is generally lower than the, best performance records in other countries, and I wish to know from the minister if he considers that after the war Canada will be able to produce aircraft in competition with other countries? I noticed that when he spoke the other day in connection with post-war aviation he stated that a vigorous aeroplane construction industry was an essential complement to Canada's postwar aviation plans. I take it from that that when the war is over Canada will continue to produce planes in competition with other countries. On page 1695 of Hansard the minister placed comparative statistics on the production of Mosquitos in the United Kingdom and the United States and he said:
In this connection, I think it may be of value to place on Hansard a table showing the comparative statistics on the production of the Mosquito in the United Kingdom and in Canada. In giving these figures I ask you to remember that the design originated with the English company.
Then he gave figures to show that in nineteen months after commencement of manufacture the cumulative totals of aircraft accepted in Canada and England were nine and five respectively.

I thought I attempted to make it clear when I spoke last time that those figures were for one plant in England, as against one plant here, apparently the de Havilland parent plant in England as against the de Havilland plant in Canada. There are other plants in England producing this machine.

I took it as a comparison between the best plant in England and the Canadian production; is that correct?

War Appropriation-Supplies
I would not say for sure, but it is probably the best plant. It is the plant that started as we did to produce the first Mosquito plane.
The comparison does not give the picture. If the choice of the English factory is not the choice of the best factory in production over there-
It may be. I do not know. It is the one which has been operating the longest.

How many employees are there in the United Kingdom plant as compared with the number in the Canadian plant? That is a matter which must be known before these statistics become worth while at all. Has the minister that information?

I think we have it. In any event, the de Havilland plant is one of the biggest plants in England. It has been in production since the beginning of the war. I dare say it would have the more employees. But I think you would have to go farther and say how many employees were working on the Mosquito, just as at the Toronto de Havilland it is a question of how many employees are working on the Mosquito. We were on other planes when we were starting production of the Mosquito. I think the hon. member is getting into pretty deep water when he asks for that information.

These statistics
mean nothing as they stand on the record unless it is known how many men in the United Kingdom factory were employed on Mosquitos when compared with the numbers in Canada. That is the point I make in connection with these particular figures which are given, that they may provide a fair comparison; they may be entirely meaningless unless we have information as to the numbers.

Let me put it to my hon. friend in this way. The Mosquito, when it was accepted, was an exceedingly important plane. I think both put on all the men they could use, but how many they put on I do not know. I would find it difficult to ascertain that here in Canada.

I am not entering into an argument at the moment, but I am pointing out that statistics like those on page 1695 are as meaningless as some of the promises of production which were made by the minister in 1942.

Let us be a little sensible about that. I put the table on Hansard as a matter of information. It means exactly

what is said. It says the performance in the British plant was so much and the performance of the Canadian plant-not my predictions of performance-was so much. I gave the best information I could. Let my hon. friend make the best out of it. If he suggests that anyone connected with the production of aeroplanes in this country is not doing the best he can, let him give us the name and we will consider the situation. This snarling around and trying to make points out of nothing is getting rather tiresome.

Let me tell the minister this, that in so far as certain types of production are concerned there can be no argument that his predictions made each successive year have not been borne out at all by the performance; and naturally he becomes annoyed,
Give me the predictions I made last year, and see if they have been borne out or not.

I will refer to that in a moment. Naturally he becomes annoyed. That is always the refuge of the minister in this regard. In November, 1942, he made the statement that three Mosquitos a day would be produced in 1943.
Can the hon. member read that statement to me?

The minister to Australia at the same time made the statement that "In 1943 we will be producing five per day." These predictions did not come true. Then .the minister comes along on March 21 and places on record the performance in England and the performance in Canada, but does not give the man-power in each engaged on the production of one aeroplane or more, so that the comparison is not helpful to this committee.
I pass on to a matter connected with the improvement of performance and production. Two or three years ago a committee was set up under Mr. Hirst to encourage production and performance. During the past two years another committee has been in operation engaged in encouraging production. It was set up on December 10, 1941. The order creating it states that it was desirable to carry on a campaign of publicity and public education designed to promote and develop a full realization of the gravity of the existing emergency and the necessity of individual and united effort, cooperation and responsibility in order that Canada's participation in the war might be of maximum effectiveness. In that year, Cockfield, Brown and Company Limited

War Appropriation-&upplies
were placed in charge of the advertising campaign, and they accepted that position without remuneration. During the first year the expenditure amounted, I believe, to around $150,000. I ask the minister now, how was that expenditure justified? In 1942 it was extended for a further year, and on March 30. 1943, it was extended for another year. The order in council extending it for the further year stated that the expenditure upon the campaign from its inception to March 31, 1943, will amount to 8237,000. What is the idea, I should like to ask the minister, after we have already set up a war information board designed to improve morale, to set up a further organization in the minister's department on which the expenditure to the end of March, 1943, was 8237,000, and to which a further amount of $125,000 was allotted for the last year. I ask the minister to explain what has been done with a sum of approximately S360.000 expended under order in council P.C. 9635 and subsequent ones. Who has been in charge of this? Why has it been necessary to make this expenditure under the Department of Munitions and Supply instead of through the war information board or one of the other boards connected with wartime information? It seems to me that that is a very considerable sum to be expended on the improvement of morale in one department when we already have the war information board and other instruments of information engaged in that connection.
I pass on now to post-war aircraft production. It was referred to by the hon. member for York West. The minister made a speech in Washington in December last-
I have never made a speech in Washington in my life.

The minister was talking to reporters, and the report indicates that it has all the appearances of a speech. He said that the business of transforming from war-time to peace-time manufacture should not be long and would be carried out in stages. Canadian aircraft production could easily be transformed to meet the demands of commercial passenger and freight carrying needs. Mr. Bell, director of aircraft production, in a statement of February 11, 1944, stated that our aircraft industry has bonclusively demonstrated that it is capable of building the largest and most complicated types of operational aircraft in the world. He stressed the necessity of building now in order to ensure the permanent future of this nationally important industry. He says that in order to build up the industry it is necessary that design staffs capable of competing with the 100-1184
world be set up and that manufacturing costs competitive with those of Britain and the United States be established.
I would ask the minister to give the committee and the country a picture with regard to the continuance of these aircraft factories after the war is over. Some 122,000 men and women are engaged in production. Starting almost from scratch, the training of these workers has been a remarkable piece of work. I have visited nearly all of the aircraft plants in the country, and one thing that amazes me is the way in which the men have been trained to do the precision work they do to-day, considering the fact that many of them had never been connected with industry before.
When the war is over, what is to ibe done to ensure the continuance of the industry? I was rather disturbed by the statement made in November 1943, by Frederick Smye, executive assistant to the director general of aircraft production. When referring to the post-war period he was far from hopeful as to the condition of affairs. The hon. member for York West mentioned that we were not producing engines in Canada. Well, in the post-war period, according to Sir Archibald Sinclair, air minister in Great Britain, one of the most important developments in connection with air craft production will be the production of jet-propelled planes. He says it will revolutionize industry.
I would ask the minister whether consideration is now being given to the post-war period in the production of jet-propelled planes, which, it is believed, will in a large measure take the place of planes of the present types. To what extent can any of these factories be turned to the production of helicopters? According to an aeronautics board in the United States, when the war is over they will be used more than any other type of, aeroplane in inter-urban traffic. These are matters that interest the workers in these factories, and it is necessary that they be considered in determining whether or not this great industry that has been built up in war time will in fact be utilized, when peace comes, as a means of ensuring employment and also of establishing Canada's position in the post-war air world.
The minister, in his address on post-war aviation, averred that it was the policy of the government to ensure the production of civilian planes in Canada. I would ask him to enlarge on that and indicate what the plans are. I do not expect them in detail, but I do expect some indication from all the planning committees that have been set up
War Appropriation-Supplies

with regard to the post-war period so that we may know the numbers the minister believes may reasonably be employed in the aircraft industry when the -war is over.
In connection with civil aviation in Canada I would also ask to what extent expansion will take place so as to employ the 25,000 referred to by Doctor George Weir in his report on the post-war.
All of us are pleased, with the increase in production of aircraft, and most of us feel that the use of trained personnel in the post-war should not be lost sight of by lack of planning now.

Apparently there are two
outstanding questions, one of which is: Why did the department interest itself in personnel work? Every production organization in every allied country has carried on programmes of the type that has been carried on by the Department of Munitions and Supply. The programme to which the hon. member referred was not confined to aircraft production. It covered the entire field of war production. The expenditure was not great in proportion to the size of our programme, measured by similar expenditures in any other country. It had nothing in particular to do with the work of the war information board except that it was coordinated with the work of that body. The purpose of our expenditure was intended to reach the personnel of war plants, whereas the purpose of the war information board is to reach all the people of Canada and of countries outside Canada.
The money has been well spent. Most plants have a plant publication put out by the employees, and part of the service is to provide up-to-date news for plant publications and to encourage their production. Another object has been to bring information home from the front lines regarding the use of a particular product. When a submarine is sunk it is a matter of interest to the men and women who were engaged in building the corvette that sank that submarine, or in building components of that corvette, to have that news in pictorial form.
Then there is the matter of plant entertainment in plants in more isolated communities. A good deal has been done in the making and distribution of moving pictures and providing projection equipment for the plants. Also, it has been found that for many types of production music in the plant during working hours has a stimulating effect on the workers and prevents fatigue. That has been introduced into plants.
(Mr. Diefenbaker.]
That covers generally the scope of the work. It is well established to-day, and expenditures are dropping materially. Expenditures will be much less for the current year than previously.
The results are wholly intangible. One man could argue that there have been no results, while another could argue that the results have been excellent. I do not care to enter into that sort of argument. I am always a sceptic in matters I do not understand, and I should not like to appear as a witness as to whether the results obtained in the morale building campaign were worth the money or not. That will have to remain a matter of opinion.
As far as the future of the aircraft industry is concerned, that of course is a very large question indeed. If my hon. friend, or anyone else, could tell me when the problem will arise and what the conditions at that time will be, it would be very much easier to forecast the future. If I were sure that the war would stop in July of this year, I might be able to give an answer. If the war should go on for two more years the answer I gave to-day would certainly be used against me by the hon. member if he and I were both in the house at the time, because the situation then would be so different that my answer then would probably be different.
We are paying some attention to the postwar situation. We have a cargo plane in production here, and have had for some two years. It was an excellent cargo plane before the war, is still the best of its type, and will certainly continue to be produced to meet post-war requirements.
Is that the Norseman?

Yes. We have taken what we believe to be the plane most likely to succeed in the next five years, the Douglas DC-4. We have obtained manufacturing rights for that plane, and manufacturing has been started at the government-owned plant operated by Canadian Vickers at Montreal. That will certainly be a post-war project. Two intermediate types of planes are required as between those two, a small transport plane and a medium transport plane. Several designs are being studied, and out of them will come two or three types which should have substantial use in this country, and which can be put into production quickly.
We are also interested in a transatlantic type of plane. The design for that is well advanced, and it is probable that that may be added to the types of planes which will be produced post-war.

Is it of Canadian design?

War Appropriation-Supplies

Combination, Canadian and British. So much for types of planes.
As far as engines are concerned we are in a happy position. Up to this time, we have never had an airframe awaiting an engine. We have always been able to obtain the engines we have required during a very tight period of supply. We are now coming to a period where engine production will be well ahead of requirements, and, not being tied to any particular engine of Canadian manufacture, we can go out and buy any engine in the world, and buy it on favourable terms. So that the necessity for using one particular engine is not a problem to our designers. It would be unfortunate if it were so, because aeroplane engines are subject to frequent changes. It takes three or four years of experiments to bring out a new type of engine, and by the time manufacture is started the designers would know of a better engine that could be built. Large expenditures are devoted to development work. Production is in great quantity when the new type arrives. We in Canada have the choice of the production of both the United States and Great Britain. As my hon. friend has stated, it is quite likely that aeroplane engines as we know them to-day are becoming obsolescent. We are not sure of that, but there is a suspicion that that is so.
For the past two years Canada has been actively associated with the development of the new type engine, the jet-propulsion engine. We have had a strong team in England working with the designers of the engine, and with three or four plants which are engaged in development wTork. Part of the development work has been moved to Canada. We are conducting cold-weather experiments on the various types of jet-propulsion engines as they are produced, to determine the relative merits of each type under conditions of extreme weather. I can assure hon. members that we shall be in a position to start from scratch in the development of jet-propulsion engines. We are capable of starting on even terms with other countries and since no one will have any particular advantage in the building of jet-propulsion engines, I think we should be warranted in undertaking engine-building with some prospect of success.

There are several questions I wish to ask the minister. I think he will realize that when the estimates of the war ministers were under review it was understood that much of the money they were asking the house to vote was to be spent by the Department of Munitions and Supply, so that we have to direct our questions to the minister of that department.
The first question I wish to raise is this: What provision has the government made for ensuring accuracy as to the cost of planes and other goods produced on the cost-plus type of contract? I am told by engineers in many plants that in estimating the cost of this production the government is obliged to depend on the records and books of the companies engaged in this business; that the only inspectors the government has of costs are the accountants and bookkeepers who check the records of the firms producing these goods, that there are not in many plants engineers or technical men who are capable of telling how many machines are required for the production of a special job, how much of machine tools is require, and what number of man-hours should go into the job, and that the government is pretty much at the mercy of the records of private companies in this matter. Would the minister make a statement on that?
Second is the question of subcontracts. Has the government any check on the letting of subcontracts, either with reference to the efficiency of the firm that received the contract, or with reference to the costs charged for these contracts? Here again I am hearing continually that subcontracts are passed on from two or three individuals. I heard of one instance where a subcontract had changed hands seven times and only the seventh man received the contract andi produced the goods, and that in each instance there was a profit of some kind charged.

I think that is information which my hon. friend is in duty bound to give the government. If that happened; if there were six rake-offs in subcontracts, the government should certainly know it and be in a position to prosecute. Is my hon. friend prepared to give the names?
I can give the minister the name of the plant in which the contract was let. The difficulty is that the men in those plants are under oath not to give information.
Then how do you know?

My hon. friend is mistaken. He has been dragging his line into deep water unless he can prove his statement that a contract has passed through six hands before the goods were finally produced. It is his duty as a member to give his proof of that statement.

I am simply asking-

The hon. member said he knew of his own knowledge what happened. Let him not shift his ground. There must be some sense of responsibility on the part of a member speaking in this house. The hon. member has made a statement and I have asked for the names.
My statement is that I was told by a responsible man of contracts-this is common information around the town^-

Let us make it common information here. If you have information it is your duty to give it to this committee. Unless you are prepared to give the name of the man from whom you obtained the information, or unless you are prepared to give the hands through which it passed, you are not giving information but just spreading mud. I think that is what you are doing. You have made a definite charge on that point. Now give us the information.
Mr. NOSEWORTHY': I did not make the definite statement that it happened. I made the statement that I have been told that this sort of thing is going on. I have no means of investigating it. The minister has every chance of investigating these things. I am asking the minister what check his department has on the giving of subcontracts. I think if he investigates he will find that numbers of subcontracts are let more than once, and that in many cases it is not the man who first receives the subcontract who finally produces the goods.

I deny that absolutely. If my hon. friend can give me one example, of a subcontract being sublet twice or three times, or any other number of times-I will not insist upon seven times-I will apologize to him on the floor of the house.

I have to accept the minister's statement and assume that he has sufficient checks to see that this does not happen. I shall see if I can get definite information and give the minister examples as to where I have been informed this has happened.
Another question I should like to ask the minister pertains to a matter which came to my attention in Saint John, with regard to shipbuilding. When I was there in October shipbuilders employed in the harbour brought to my attention the fact that a superintendent, I think brought down from the Toronto Shipbuilding company, ordered practically all the carpenters working on that ship to set about building a superstructure over the deck, notwithstanding the fact that practically all the deck work has been done, and the further
[Mr. Noseworthv.l
fact that these men were accustomed to build ships during the fall and winter months without the protection of any deck structure. My information, gathered at that time, was that practically all the carpenters were taken off the ship and put to work building this structure; that trusses were erected over the deck of the ship; that the legs of those trusses were set in sockets made of steel and welded to the deck of the ship. It was estimated by carpenters employed on that boat that about forty thousand feet of lumber was used in the construction of that structure. Panels were made of matched lumber, much of it long lengths of Douglas fir, matched spruce, four by four timbers and so on. About a month later I learned that practically all the carpenters working on the ships at that point were called in to rush this structure to completion, and that within a matter of days after it was finished the same men were called in to dismantle it because the ship was required to make a trial run, and could not make it with that structure superimposed upon the deck. It was a matter of considerable criticism among carpenters and shipbuilders there, and I think the minister should give us some information on the subject.
There is another matter to which I wish to direct the attention of the minister. Here again I do not want him to consider that I am making a charge against his department. I am passing on to him information that has been given to me.

Is my hon. friend prepared to take the responsibility for the information he is giving? If he is. not prepared to take that responsibility, then I suggest he should not give it. My hon. friend is simply spreading gossip as fact.
Has the minister started to make a new set of rules for this house?
No.
Any hon. member can bring any matter before the minister and ask him to look into it.
Sit down.
I will not sit down.
I have the floor.
While I am on my feet might I suggest that the minister might start addressing the Chair instead of saying "you" across the floor of the chamber.
