I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that my hon. friend is drawing upon all the gossip he has picked up around the country, and is giving it in this house as facts. When an hon. member makes a statement in the house I think he must assume responsibility for it. My hon. friend made the statement here to-day that contracts are passed through six or seven hands before the work is performed. That is a very serious statement. If it were true, my department would deserve from the people of Canada the greatest censure that could be imagined. It is not true; it is wholly untrue, but the hon. member makes the statement. Now he proposes to make another statement. He does not know whether or not it is true; it is just something people have told him. Is this the place to retail irresponsible gossip?

The minister knows very well that hon. members have the greatest difficulty in getting accurate information. Rumours can be heard all across this country; I am sure every hon. member must have heard, from men working in various plants, of the things that are going on. These men are under oath not to pass on that information to anyone.

Let me settle that point. So far as I know there is no man in any plant in this country who is under oath, unless he is handling very confidential work. Let us not talk about the ordinary worker in the plant being under oath.
Then let me get back to the question. The minister objects to my asking for information on facts that have been laid before me.
You ask the questions and let me give you the facts. You are giving the facts.

On Thursday last the hon. member for Lake Centre referred to the situation at the Sutton Horsley plant at Leaside. The minister may have answered the question which was asked, but following the question there was quite a melee, and though I looked through Hansard I could not find any answer or explanation by the minister in regard to the situation prevailing there. To-day I have a letter from the president and secretary of lodge 1673 of the International Association of Machinists, which operates in that plant, and they tell me-
Read the letter and then lay it on the table.
I am quite prepared to read this letter.
Never mind explaining it.

It is written on
behalf of the employees and reads:
We, the employees of Sutton Horsley Limited, Leaside, Ontario, members of Local 1673 of the International Association of Machinists, strongly protest the chaotic condition existing in our plant which is engaged in a vital war industry of manufacturing aircraft instruments, the most important plant of its kind in Canada.
In March, 1943, R. J. Pinchin was appointed by order in council as controller of above company, as we understood, to build this company up. During his controllership things have gone from bad to worse to the extent that out of approximately 1,200 employees we now have less than 400, with layoffs continuing from day to day and rumours that the plant will close down in about six weeks.
It is needless to emphasize the moral effect this has upon the workers in the plant and their families whose sons, husbands and brothers are fighting for the Four Freedoms. This condition is inconsistent with a total war effort and also shows the complete lack of preparation towards a post-war plan of work and security.
This letter is signed by the president and the secretary of the union. I do not know these men, but I draw the matter to the minister's attention, and ask if he will make a statement as to prevailing conditions in that plant.
Who signed the letter?
Do the rules of the committee require that that be given?
Oh, yes.
They certainly do.
My hon. friend has read the letter. Of course he will table it; that is always done. He need not worry about it, because I got a letter, too. I could table that, as well.
I do not think the rules of the house require it; although I believe there is no objection to tabling the letter. I believe the hon. member will do it, voluntarily.

If my hon. friend will read Hansard he will find I made a statement a few days ago respecting the situation at that plant. The fact of the matter is that the plant is making instruments for trainer aircraft. The production of trainer aircraft has dropped very sharply and quickly. The result is that fewer instruments are required, and therefore Sutton Horsley is called upon to make fewer instruments. The fact of the controller's being appointed has not much to do with the volume of work. The purpose in having the controller was to straighten out
War Appropriation-Supplies

an unsatisfactory financial condition. That has been done, and Sutton Horsley are doing all the work we have for them to do, and will continue to do so.
Will the minister make a statement respecting the other points mentioned?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I can answer the hon. member's first question, namely as to the checks or controls we had over cost-plus contracts. Last year I made a statement in the house respecting the nature of contracts, and the whole purchasing method in the Department of Munitions and Supply. If the hon. member will turn to page 3646 of Hansard he will find what those checks are. To speak succinctly, they are three in number, the first of which is the cost accountant, the next the representative of the Department of Munitions and Supply, and the third is the director-general of the programme. Those three officers exercise checks over cost-plus contracts.
The cost accountant is, of course, an officer of the treasury branch, and works hand in hand with our officers. They are found in all our plants across the country. There are hundreds of such cost accountants, in the plants. That officer works in conformity with a strict formula which I placed on Hansard on, the occasion to which I have referred, giving those things which can be charged as items of cost, and those which could not be so charged. Then I believe the war expenditures committee made a finding that there were not nearly enough cost accountants, and every effort was being made to obtain as many as could be found.
Then, in each plant there is a representative of the Department of Munitions and Supply. Those representatives are officers of our department who worked in conjunction with the cost accountants. Finally, there were the directors-general of each of the programmes in the department.
Those three officers exercised a check or control over cost-plus contracts. Then the hon. member asked a question regarding subcontracts, but I am not in a position to give him the details he sought. He will find that at the last session of parliament the house gave the Department of Munitions and Supply certain powers over subcontracts. That was done under the Department of Munitions and Supply Act. I believe there he will find set out a number of the powers possessed by the department with reference to subcontracts.

I have never questioned the fact that there are a number of cost accountants to inspect the contracts. But has

the government in those plants engineers who are competent to know whether too many machines or too many tools are being used, or whether too much time has been charged against a government job? Are there any engineers who know what should go into a construction job?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Yes; in almost all plants across Canada there is a resident representative from the Department of Munitions and Supply, and he remains in the plant.

Since the hon. member for York South has been making statements which have been questioned, I should like to take a few minutes of the time of the committee to correct a statement he made in the house on Thursday afternoon of last week. The statement to which I refer is found at page 1785 of Hansard for March 23, where the disposition of the plant at Nobel, Ontario, is being discussed. After the hon. member had described the plant at some length he said this, respecting the industry at Nobel.
The industry is the only industry between Orillia and Sudbury, a distance of from 175 to 180 miles, the only one from Georgian bay to Pembroke, a strategic position for a peace-time industry.
I understand the hon. member for York South is a schoolteacher, and if he did not know from his knowledge of geography that that was a misstatement, then he should have known from his knowledge of the district. He must know that within the area he mentioned lies practically the whole of the district of Muskoka, and he must know, too, that there are three good-sized towns in that area, namely Gravenhurst, Bracebridge and Huntsville, each of which has industries.
Had the hon. member taken the time or the trouble to find out whether or not there were any industries in that district, he would have found that in the town of Huntsville there is a large tannery operated by the Anglo-Canadian Leather company, the largest producer of sole leather in the British empire. He would have found out further, that in that town there is a large mill and factory operated by the Muskoka Woods company, which claims to be the largest manufacturer of birch and maple hardwood flooring in Canada.
Coming south to the town of Bracebridge, he would have found, among other industries too numerous to mention, the Bird Woollen company, the quality of whose products has a nationwide reputation. Coming down to Gravenhurst, he would have found the Rubber-set company, whose products are marketed throughout Canada and part of the United States. In addition to these, it might be of interest for him to know that the boatbuilders

War Appropriation-Supplies
in Muskoka, at Bracebridge, Graven-hurst, Port Carling and Honey Harbour have completed nineteen Fairmiles for the British and Canadian- navies. The Fairmile is 112 feet long with a beam of eighteen feet and a top speed of twenty-five miles an hour. It is a splendid craft. In addition to that they have contracts for two mine-sweepers of much larger dimensions. Besides these craft they have completed some 600 smaller craft, including motor-boats, live-saving boats and other types. That is not a bad showing for a district represented by the hon. member as having no industries whatever. I think the statement he made is a reflection upon the enterprise of -the people I have the honour to represent. I could not let it pass without comment and I know the people I represent would not want me to. I do not know what his intention- was in making such a statement unless he intended to convey the idea that if the plant at Nobel was not put in operation again there would -be no industry to absorb these people.
I have listened to hon. members criticizing the industries which have grown up during the last thirty-five years and I cannot help thinking what the course of the war would have been had those gentlemen been on this side of the house and in control of the government. What would have happened if they had dictated the war policy of this country? We know what their policy has been. I shall not go over it again since it has been placed on Hansard many times. At a time when Great Britain faced her greatest crisis; at a time when she was suffering for the cause of freedom-to an extent never equalled by any other nation, we know they would have denied- the people of Great Britain the consolation of knowing there was an air force, a navy and an army being prepared in this country with feverish haste to go to their assistance at the earliest possible moment. No one can say what the course of war might have been if the people of Great Britain had not known they had the support of the first nation in the British commonwealth of nations outside of Great Britain.
I wish to say a word on behalf of the Minister of Munitions and Supply. This is not my word alone; I am passing on the word that comes to me from everyone in my riding with whom I have talked. He is doing a first-class job. Those same words can be said of every member of the cabinet who has anything to do with the war. I have heard friends of mine who are strong Conservatives say that this government is doing a first-class job, and I agree with them. In place of criticizing things that have no bearing upon the course 100-119
of the war, we should be ready to give more credit to the government for what they are doing.

In reply to the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario may I say that I am sure the people of his constituency will appreciate the way he has come to the defence of his district. Perhaps I should have qualified my statement. When I referred to industry in that district I was referring to the plant at Nobel, which I contended should be retained as a peace-time industry. I have no doubt that the hon. member who has just spoken and all the people in his constituency will agree that there is a great need for a large peace-time industry in that district. I know of no part of Ontario that suffered more in the years before the war because of a lack of employment than the district represented by the hon. member.

I should like to ask the minister a question. This is not intended as criticism but is merely a means of getting information which I think will be interesting to all members of the house. This question may have been asked previously, although I did not hear it when I was in the house, nor could I find it in Hansard. What is the present position of the Canol project? Is it to be completed? There has been a good deal of discussion about this and I have not heard a definite statement as to just what is the present situation.

I do not know whether I can give my hon. friend the information he requires. The Canol project is a United States project. The only part Canada has in it is that we allow the use of certain of our territory for exploration purposes, and have permitted the United States government to build a pipeline and refinery on Canadian territory. As far as I know the work is in progress.

Have we any interest in the ultimate disposition of the project if it is to be completed? If it is completed it seems to me that it will have some bearing upon the matters we are discussing, because it would affect the supply of oil and so on.
The regulations have been tabled and I do not think there is anything new to report. It does not come within the orbit of my department.
Has it been completed?

I think the pipeline has been completed and the refinery is in operation. I do not know that the project itself can ever be completed, but I presume that it is being enlarged.

War Appropriation-Supplies
Has it been completed up to the point it was intended to complete it?
We had better let the hon. member for Yukon answer since he knows all about it.

The government has already announced the terms upon which the Canol project is being carried on. I understand that at a certain time after the war representatives of Canada and the United States will value the project. If Canada does not choose to buy it within a certain time, then it will be sold by public tender. The pipeline is only a four-inch line. I understand that it is completed and that the refinery is in a fair way to get into operation in May. Further than that I cannot say anything.

Perhaps I could add a word to that. There was an exchange of notes between Canada and the United States covering the development. Then regulations were issued in connection with certain areas and were tabled in the house at the last session. Those regulations set out the conditions under which Imperial Oil are operating. The arrangements that Imperial Oil have with the United States war department are, of course, a matter between that company and the war department of the United States.

This is in Canadian territory and surely we should be able to get some information about a project of this dimension. Just what is the situation? Has the project been successful in finding sufficient oil to justify the operation of a refinery? Are we interested in the project, as is indicated by the documents tabled at the last session? I ask these questions innocently because I wish to be able to satisfy requests for information which I receive from people who are interested in this particular project.

I think my hon. friend will recognize just as quickly as anyone in the house that the United States war department are interested through arrangements made with Imperial Oil in a development that was undertaken for the purpose of ensuring a certain oil supply for defence purposes in the northwestern part of Canada and of Alaska. That was undertaken at a time when the Japanese menace looked a great deal more threatening than it is to-day. I do not know how far the government are at liberty to disclose arrangements which involve the government of the United States through its war department. The regulations, which after all are the important thing so far as this country is concerned, were 
tabled; that is, the conditions under which Imperial Oil undertook the developments. So far as the pipeline is concerned, I believe that it is completed, but I am not in a position to say at the moment whether oil is going from Norman wells to the refinery at White Horse because I have not at the moment information on that particular point. But the whole matter was one which was entered into between the government of Canada and the government of the United States, and if my memory is right, the understanding which was covered by the exchange of notes has already been given to the house. However, my memory on this point may be at fault! If the exchange of notes has not been tabled, there is a very goofi reason, because the Canadian government would have to have an agreement with the government of the United States on a matter of that kind.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
The remarks I have to make I would prefer to make when the minister is present.
I am always present.

This afternoon, on the orders of the day, I endeavoured to get from the minister an answer as briefly and as explicitly as possible with regard to this question of closing plants in the maritime provinces. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) answered most of that question, but I was not quite satisfied with the replies he gave. As the minister is well aware, there is considerable reason for unrest and apprehension in the maritime provinces with respect to the closing of plants. Not very much industry has been created in those three provinces as a result of the war, and there was very little there prior to the outbreak of the war. During the session of the house, from different sections of the maritime provinces, telegrams of protest and inquiries are being sent in.
The question I attempted to raise this afternoon had reference to the closing down of the Clark Ruse aircraft plant both in Nova Scotia and in New Brunswick. The Minister of Labour, in his reply, ridiculed, in my opinion, those who were sending in the telegrams of protest and tried to make it appear that one man sent in the telegrams and that there was no one in the organization he represented who held the views he expressed in that telegram. I

War Appropriation-Supplies
believe the hon. member for York West asked a question on Friday and read a telegram into the records.
No. He did not read a telegram into the record; he just referred to it.

He summarized it. I did not
base my question this afternoon on that particular telegram. The fact is, that I sent that telegram across the floor of the house to the Minister of Labour and asked him if he would check it up and determine whether there was merit in the proposals which it contained with respect to the procedure of lay-off. In addition to that telegram, I had a shower of other messages over the week-end from men, some of whom I know personally and for whom I have a good deal of respect, and the telegrams I received from Moncton and from the province of Nova Scotia were not quarrelling with the administration of the selective service regulations.
We know, and the senders of the telegrams know, that under the selective service regulations a certain definite road must be followed with respect to lay-offs, but the inquiries and the protests I received were as to the future of these plants in Nova Scotia, and as to whether the government had a policy with regard to the utilization of the Clark Ruse aircraft plants in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. That, I submit, is a question to which the Minister of Munitions and Supply should give an answer to the members of this house.
The Minister of Labour, in his remarks this afternoon, breezily brushed to one side the question of men being laid off, with the observation that a large percentage of them were going into the armed services and would be immediately called up as they were laid off. That I think is a bad answer and a bad attitude to take. If the only redress that the government has to offer men who are being displaced in industry in the maritime provinces, because of the closing down of these industries, is the answer, "Oh, well; immediately you are put out of a job in those provinces we will call you up to the armed services and give you the privilege of going overseas and fighting for the country," it is not a solution. It is a callous way of putting the thing, and one which I think was ill-advised on the part of the Minister of Labour.
What we are concerned to know is whether, after the crown has created these plants at considerable expense to the taxpayers, it is not possible now to utilize both the plant in Moncton and the plant in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, for other purposes. I feel that all the 100-1191
members from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island, have, on this particular question, a definite responsibility to those provinces.
These plants were built up, as the minister pointed out, for the purpose of aircraft repairs. and a few days ago he made a statement in the house to the effect that Canada expects to play a definite and important part in civil aviation after the war is over. If that is true, then both the Dartmouth plant and the Moncton plant are strategically located. There are large aerodromes which no doubt will be used in that civil aviation project, and these repair plants would, I think, fit quite definitely into a scheme of servicing aircraft after the war.	[DOT]
Practically every newspaper that one has picked up in the last four or five months has carried a story about the closing down of something in the way of industry in the maritime provinces. During the last session of the house we heard of shipbuilding plants that had been built up-Ferguson Brothers, for example, where there w'ere partly completed boats, with sufficient material to complete them, and overnight the order was cancelled. Partly completed tugs were put on board the train and shipped to Montreal to be completed, and the materials were taken away. Next we hear of the Trenton shell plant. That is down and twelve hundred or thirteen hundred men are thrown out of employment. There is a good deal of the taxpayer's money in that plant. It is just another shut-down.
Telegrams now tell us that aircraft plants are being closed down, and picking up another press clipping of March 22 we find that they are laying off the entire female personnel of Enamel and Heating Products Limited of Sackville, New Brunswick. The whole story all along the line, as far as the industrial setup in the maritime provinces is concerned, is a matter of going out of production and laying off people, leaving them idle, and no one apparently has plans for the utilization of these plants or of the equipment, or for seeing whether they can be used in the future. It is just a matter of closing them out.
The minister this afternoon made a statement with respect to the fuel policy and definitely stated that certain subsidies are to be established in the west and that a royal commission is to be appointed for the purpose of examining the whole fuel situation of western Canada with the end in view of establishing a peace-time fuel policy in the western provinces. When the hon. member for York-Sunbury asked him whether the Minto field and the fields of eastern Canada
War Appropriation-Supplies

were to be included in this royal commission's probe, with a view to developing a fuel policy for -the future, I at least understood the minister to say that the eastern end of the country was not to be included in the investigation.

No. I announced a subsidy policy for western Canada, and I said that consideration had been given to revision of subsidies for the Minto field and that I expected to make a statement on that subject within a day or two. I said that the subsidy situation in Nova Scotia is being studied. As a matter of fact, we have called in experts to make a report on the Nova Scotia situation. I said definitely that the royal commission is for all Canada, to review the coal policy for all Canada and recommend such changes as the situation may call for.

I beg the minister's pardon. I understood that in replying to the hon. member for York-Sunbury he was referring to the terms of reference of the royal commission to be appointed. I am very glad indeed that the minister has decided to have a complete examination made of the whole fuel situation by a royal commission with a view to recommending a national fuel policy that will be carried into the post-war period. This is a step in the right direction, and I compliment the minister upon taking it.
What I particularly rose to question the minister about to-night was the pulling out of established industries in Nova Scotia. I should like to hear from the minister whether the government has any policy with regard to using the shell plant at Trenton, if not for the production of shells, for any other purpose for which the plant can be used.
I would also like to know what is to be the future of the two aircraft plants at Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, and Lakeburn, New Brunswick. I think the people of the maritime province are entitled to an answer. If these plants are to oe closed, the people have a right to know t, so that they can make other arrangements. If they are not to be closed but can be refooled and used for some other purpose, the people who are dependent on these plants as i means of livelihood have a right to know it.
I see the Minister of Labour is here. I made a few remarks in his absence, and so that there may be no misunderstanding I should like him to hear exactly what I had to say. I think the Minister of Labour in his reply to a question this afternoon was not very happy in his answer. I consider that his answer was breezy, ill-advised and ill-considered.
But otherwise all right?

I refer to this statement with respect to these plants being virtually closed

and some three hundred men being laid off at both of them, that selective service was handling the problem as prescribed by the regulations-with that I do not quarrel-and that there was not much to worry about because a large percentage of these men, immediately after losing their employment in the aircraft plants, would be called up for military service. That is the part of his answer with which I quarrel. It was an unhappy remark. It does not induce a very good frame of mind in a man entering the armed service.
My hon. friend does not object to a man defending his country, does he?
I certainly do not, and I do not think anybody would understand me as saying that. The impression of the minister's statement on my mind and on that of the average man-
Oh, no.

Well, then, say below the average. If I were employed in one of these Clark Ruse plants-and remember I know many of these men who, during the days between the two wars never had a job at all- this is how I would feel. I would say to myself: "I have a family. I have accepted the obligations of doing what I could in the field of production"

a lot of these men were trained for that purpose. Overnight, orders come to close the plant and my job is gone. There is no other job for me to go to in that part of the country because industry which had started up there by virtue of the war has closed down. Now I am told to report to the selective service office. The selective service officer advises me to report for duty. I am not enlisting voluntarily. I am not being given an opportunity to decide for myself whether I am going to fight for my country. In effect I am being forced into the service by virtue of economic circumstances. I am leaving my country to go into military service because there is no job here for me, because a member of the government, who is responsible, makes the observation in the house when discussing this question that that is the solution of the problem caused by the closing down of plants in the maritime provinces.
That is not a very happy frame of mind with which to send a man into the armed services. Certainly it is not a solution of the problem of scrapping industries in a section of the country that is badly in need of stimulation for industry. Is that to be the attitude not only with respect to those now losing their employment, but with respect to post-war employment when the men return from overseas?
