In order to clarify things and satisfy the people of the maritimes, who are viewing the situation very seriously, the Minister of Munitions and Supply should make a definite statement one way or the other, so that we may know what to expect in the future and on the basis of that may be able to regulate our lives. If it' is the intention to siphon off everyone from that section of the country who is able to work, and bring them into the central provinces, we have a right to know it so that we can make arrangements to move our families and live somewhere else. The trend of events, as I have seen it in the past year at least in the maritime province, is to pull out all war industry that has been created there. There is no thought of expansion or development of that industry but rather the closing of it down. Would the minister make a statement on that question?

I too, like the hon. member for Cape Breton South, have received telegrams in connection with the closing of the Clark Ruse plant at Dartmouth, and so has my colleague the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Macdonald). We were naturally concerned because the plant is in our constituency, just as we would be concerned by the closing of plants in any part of Nova Scotia, which would naturally receive our attention. We discussed the matter together, but we did not bring those telegrams here on Friday afternoon and place them before the minister on the orders of the day; we felt there was another procedure which perhaps would give us a better understanding of the situation. My colleague and I got in touch with officials of the Department of Munitions and Supply, who went rather fully into the background of the plant at Dartmouth, as to the purpose for which it was first brought into being. We were told that it was established for the purpose of overhauling and repairing aeroplanes of the type that were used on the Atlantic coast, and we were further informed that a change had been made in the kind of aeroplane used there. I need not give the names of the planes, but we were given that information, I considered in a confidential way, and that was the reason for the situation which then existed at that plant. The Royal Canadian Air Force notified the Department of Munitions and Supply of the change that was to be made in the type of planes to be used, and steps were taken immediately to cut down the number of men employed there because, as they stated frankly, they did not think the people of Canada would want three or four or five hundred men employed for a certain period of time unless there was actually work for them to do, particularly when these men could be placed in useful employment elsewhere.
That was the reason given us, but we were not entirely satisfied that we had the whole story, with due respect to those who gave us that information. Accordingly we went further.
I personally took up the matter with the Minister of Labour, who said he could assure me that these men would be placed in other positions. More than that, he said they were immediately taking steps to send officials from the selective service office at Halifax to look after the placing of these men elsewhere. He said, "These men are not going to be thrown out of employment without notice. They have received seven days notice, and even if they have no work to do they will be paid for the seven days which that notice covers." In view of the fact that there was no work for these men, and that the department was endeavouring to find work for them elsewhere, we felt that this was a reasonable stand to take, but we pursued the question further. We went to the director of aircraft production, Mr. Bell, and inquired as to what action was taken to meet the layoff of these five hundred men, and as to whether the plant would be continued even on a temporary basis. We were told that the plant would be continued for a further period of three months with about 250 employees. Then naturally we wanted to know whether the plant could not be used for some other purpose, but he did not see how that could be done nor did the Department of Munitions and Supply. We suggested that it might be used in connection with the ship repair work being carried on in the port of Halifax, but they did not think that was feasible.
I wanted to explain this to you, Mr. Chairman, and to the other members of the committee, to indicate that more than one hon... member was interested in maintaining industries in the province of Nova Scotia, that others were equally interested but approached the subject in a little different manner. I am pleased to say that we have the assurance that the plant will be held as a stand-by. The equipment will be kept there, in case it might be of use at some future date for the work for which it was brought into being, namely, the repair and overhaul of certain types of aircraft; and I am still hopeful that use will be made of this plant. I am just as much concerned as .any other hon. member that we should hold on to what industries we have in the maritimes, particularly plants in connection with aircraft and shipbuilding.
I do not wish to deal with .the other two plants mentioned by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. He referred to the closing down of the plant at Trenton, and that matter has been brought to the attention of this committee on more than one occasion. It
War Appropriation-Supplies

is under investigation at the present time, and again I say I am hopeful that something may turn up as a result of which work will be continued there. The hon. member has also brought to the attention of this committee in almost the same words the situation prevailing at Pictou in connection with the plant of Ferguson Brothers. The Minister of Munitions and Supply gave a full explanation as to why it was necessary to cancel the contract there and carry on the work elsewhere, so -that I do not think it is necessary to go into that question at the present time. I would point out that the same situation will prevail in other parts of Canada. Because of a change in the system of training, numbers of airfields in all parts of the country have been closed. We are bound to see the closing of plants, airfields and schools after we reach a certain stage in our war production- and -training, and all that has been explained. I do not think the people of Canada expect the minister or this government to carry on any plant in which men cannot be usefully employed-, particularly if they can be employed somewhere else to help in our war effort. I do not wish to be unreasonable. I want everything it is possible t-o get for Nova Scotia, but I do not think the people of that province are going to ask me or -any other hon. -member -from the mari-times' to make unreasonable requests. They do expect us to -make every effort to find out why a plant is being closed and, if possible, to have that plant continued in operation, even if only in the capacity of a stand-by plant. However, I ask the minister to bear in -mind that at Eastern Passage he has what is considered a well-equipped plant, as well as a permanent airfield which no doubt will continue in operation following the war. I suggest to him that this plant might be utilized in connection- with the T.C.A. or in so-me other worth-while peace-time effort.

I should like to point out to my hon. friend, and to all hon. -members, -that the Clark Ruse plant is not closed-. This plant was built to repair damaged aeroplanes. Obviously the work of such a plant must be in proportion to the number of damaged aircraft. At one time the plant was very busy ; in fact the capacity -has had to be enlarged from time to time. Owing to a change in operational requirements, however, recently the number of crashed aircraft has been considerably less. As a result, the -personnel of the plant has been- cut down to -the actual work requirements. I understand the reduction- in Halifax amounts to some 500 men, which leaves about 250 or 300 still employed. I understand there -has been a small reduction at Moncton as well; just how large -that has
IMr. Isnor.]
been, I do not know, but I do -not think it is particularly important. My hon-. -friend- claims that the employees in- these plants are absolutely astonished that there should be any reduction. I think they are much more intelligent than he would lead- us to believe. Surely people whose livelihood depends upon crashed aeroplanes -must know that others are not going to crash- aeroplanes in that locality at the rate they have been crashed, forever.
Were those plants not assembly plants?
They were for a time, yes.
Yes, they were.

In the early stages there were some planes being brought in from the old country and assembled there. But the main purpose of locating the plant there was to repair certain types of aircraft. That is the only purpose of the plant at this time. The equipment is laid out for certain types of aircraft. The plant carries stocks of spares for certain types of aircraft, and the job is to repair those aircraft. A very considerable part of the personnel was brought there from upper Canada for the reason that men with some training were required. Surely those who went from upper Canada to Halifax to repair damaged aircraft did- not go there under the impression that they were going to make a profession of repairing damaged aircraft in that area. They went there to do a war job, and intended to come back to where they came from when the repairs to crashed aeroplanes were finished. Those are not plants suitable for any other work; in fact repair capacity may be needed again. Damage to aircraft may increase; we may have in that area operational requirements which will again make those -plants necessary for the purpose for which they were built. [DOT]
I assume that the Halifax plant, being adjacent to the Dartmouth airport, will probably always be used as an overhaul plant for aeroplanes. Obviously, under peace-time conditions the scale of operations will not be particularly high. I find it extraordinary that an obviously temporary war-time facility should, in the mind of anyone, be converted into a permanent industry, when no such industry of that size could possibly exist in peace time.
The hon. member mentioned the plant of Ferguson Brothers at Pictou. The situation there was that the plant was equipped for ship repairs, a badly needed facility along that coast. By a chain of circumstances, none of which was intended by the department, two tugs were moved- into that plant for construction. The department thought they were to be

War Appropriation-Supplies
constructed1 in another location, but suddenly found that they turned up in the Ferguson yard. Those tugs, had they been built there, would have occupied badly needed facilities which had been created for a special purpose, a purpose having the highest priority. Might I say that the repair of ships has a far higher priority than the building of ships, because it is much more important to keep an existing ship at sea than to build a ship which could be put to sea only after a matter of months.
When it was found that the repair facilities were clogged up with a construction job, we moved the construction job out. Ferguson Brothers were very much disturbed about the situation at the time. But I shall be very glad to lay on the table a letter from Ferguson Brothers, written a year later, in which they said that they had been fully occupied with the repair work, since the tugs were moved out, and that they wished to say that I was right; that they were quite wrong, and that we were fully warranted in taking the tugs out to make way for repair, work.

I have just a word to say. It is only human nature of a certain type that when an air centre or a training centre is shut down there is diappointment. If a war industry is closed, we are disappointed. But there is another type of human nature that is not disappointed. When our shell plant at Fort William was shut down, perhaps I was a little disappointed. But to-day that plant is sold, so that instead of making shells it is going to make foodstuffs. And where is the city in Canada that would not prefer to see the manufacture of foodstuffs rather than that of shells-because there are now enough shells.
Then No. 2 training centre which we had at the head of the lakes was one of the best in Canada, and I say that because of the number of times they took the pennant. Some of the folks there thought it should be about the last closed up, because of its efficiency. But when I spoke to the Minister of National Defence for Air he asked me, "Do you know the reason why it was closed down?" I said I thought I did, but asked, "What is it?" "Because there were not enough casualties in the air." I say to the Minister of Munitions and Supply, notwithstanding any criticism the hon. member for Davenport may level at me, that we thank God that the airmen have been spared so that our training centres can be shut down. It is only a certain type of individual who will find fault with that sort of thing. I am glad that our schools are being closed, because we do not need any more aircrew, and we are going to win the war with
practically what we have now. Before we criticize the men in our war cabinet, we should know more than present expressions would seem to show.

I wish to say a few words with regard to a very serious condition in the west. I refer to the coal situation. I was pleased to hear the minister say to-night that he was causing to be set up a royal commission which would investigate the whole coal problem from the eastern to the western coast. I may say it was my understanding this afternoon that the royal commission was only going to investigate the coal condition in the west. I am glad, however, that the minister has now corrected that statement. Because of the statement which I understood the minister to make this afternoon, but which he has just now corrected, it was my intention not to discuss the coal question until we were to go into supply, and then to move an amendment which would more or less solidify the whole subject, and bring the matter to a climax.
It is necessary that the coal situation not only in western Canada but in eastern Canada as well should be dealt with, so that there might be some satisfactory conclusion. Chaos will be the result if that is not done. This amendment I intended to move when the house was going into supply:
That all the words after the word "that" to the end of the question be struck^ out and the following substituted therefor: this house consider the advisability of formulating a national fuel policy for Canada which will:
(a)	Eliminate discrimination in favour of coal imports through subsidies.
(b)	Ensure markets for Canadian coal producers.
(c)	Provide steady employment for Canadian miners and
(d)	Make provision for transportation facilities, either by way of freight rate revisions or through the renewal of subsidies which will enable Canadian miners to compete on an equitable basis of equality in Canadian markets.
I had prepared that amendment because of the very serious situation in the west. In the last few days I have been receiving telegrams and air mail letters in regard to the matter, until now I have quite a pile of them. The situation is becoming serious. I think there is a mistaken idea in the minds of many with regard to the western fuel situation. This has been created largely by remarks made, perhaps unintentionally, in this House of Commons. I believe it was the Minister of Munitions and Supply who criticized some hon. members the other day for making statements which were not well considered. I think his rebuke was well grounded, but I should like to apply his remarks to certain hon. members
/

War Appropriation-Supplies
on this side of the house. I wish to quote what the Minister of Labour had to say in regard to Alberta coal. I think he made some remarks which were very ill advised. I quote from page 1057 of Hansard, where the minister is reported as follows:
My hon. friends will understand why much of that coal particularly Alberta coal, cannot be piled. It deteriorates, falls to pieces. It is not like Nova Scotia coal.
Mr. MacNicol: It disintegrates.
Mr. Johnston (Bow Kiver): It is good coal.
The minister stated that Alberta coal is not like Nova Scotia coal, that it will not stock-pile. For a long time we in western Canada have been endeavouring to create a market for Alberta coal in Ontario and Quebec. A goodly number of dollars have been spent by the provincial government upon advertising, and a trade commission was set up in this province which spends part of its time in Ottawa and the other part in Toronto in an endeavour to build up a market for Alberta coal. This in turn creates a market for other Canadian products and provides labour for Canadian people. These are things that should be brought about.
Now the Minister of Labour comes along and knocks the props out from under that by saying that this coal will not stock-pile, that it is not like Nova Scotia coal. I have nothing to say against Nova Scotia coal, and there are other hon. members, particularly the hon. member for Cape Breton South, who can deal with that particular commodity. But Nova Scotia coal is bituminous coal; that is the only type of coal produced in Nova Scotia. We produce bituminous coal in Alberta along with other types. I have gone to some pains to investigate the heat units of bituminous coal from western Canada and of bituminous coal from eastern Canada and I find that there is practically no difference. The minister was entirely wrong when he said what he did. He either did not know the coal situation or was deliberately making a misstatement of fact, something which should not be permitted. He says that it falls to pieces, that it deteriorates. Bituminous coal from western Canada will not deteriorate and it will .stock-pile just as well as Nova Scotia coal. We should remember this when discussing this matter. Statements such as the minister made are misleading to the public. I heard coal dealers, some of them members of this house, from Ontario say that such statements are not correct.
The other kind of coal that we produce in Alberta is domestic coal, and this is found in a number of types. We get domestic coal from Drumheller, from Lethbridge, from the Saunders area and from the Coalspur area. Each of these domestic coals is an excellent

coal. If the minister was referring to that type of coal when he said that it would not stock-pile, he was entirely wrong. We in the west have had some experience in using this coal and in fact it has been shipped to Ottawa and even a few miles out from this city. A goodly number of tons have been sent down to Toronto in an endeavour to build up a wider market for our coal. Then the minister comes along and makes his statement, and the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) agrees with him by saying, "It disintegrates".

I infer from what the hon. member is saying that he charges me with criticizing Alberta coal. There is no hon. member of this House of Commons, including the hon. member, who has done more to advocate the use of Alberta coal than I have. I was partly responsible for bringing down the first 25,000 tons of Alberta coal to Toronto and other points in Ontario. The hon. member must not misquote me. When I said it disintegrates, I mean that it does disintegrate if it is not covered. I have used several carloads of this coal.

I was just going to say that on many occasions the hon. member for Davenport had commendably advocated the use of Alberta coal and the development of Alberta industries. We thank him for that; nevertheless when the minister said that it deteriorates, falls to pieces and wrill not stock-pile, the hon. member said, "It disintegrates." I do not like to make any uncomplimentary remarks about the hon. member, but I do want to stress that if this coal is kept covered, and most domestic coal is kept covered, it will keep just as well as any other type of coal.
Exactly. It does not disintegrate when under cover.

We in western Canada buy our coal in the fall, especially since the government has advocated getting in an early supply. Two years ago I put Drumheller coal into my basement in the early fall and in the spring it was just as good as when it was put in. When this coal is brought down to eastern Canada and sold to householders and kept under cover it will keep just as well as any domestic coal produced anywhere in Canada. We should not misrepresent the facts and say that this coal will not stock-pile, that it disintegrates, leaving the impression it deteriorates rapidly and soon becomes of no value. We are trying to build up a market for this coal. The bituminous coal to which I referred a moment ago is a different type entirely. This coal is

War Appropriation-Supplies
used for industrial purposes and by locomotives. I wish to refer again to what the minister is reported as having said on page 1057 of Hansard.
What minister is my hon. friend talking about?
I am talking about the Minister of Labour at this moment.

What has this to do with the estimates of the Department of Munitions and Supply? There are civil estimates which are not now under discussion covering the subsidies on coal. My hon. friend is just building up strawmen and knocking them down. No one has said that Alberta coal will not stand handling or cannot be stored. My hon. friend and everyone else in this house knows that practically every variety of coal is mined in Alberta. There is a high grade domestic coal; there is a bituminous coal and there is a low grade lignite. If he is talking about the lignite coal, then I think he will admit that it will not store. If he is talking about bituminous coal, I think it can be said that it will store. If he is talking about high grade domestic coal, of course it will store.
Of course it will.
Why not sit down and let us get on with the estimates?
Let me tell the minister that I shall not sit down until he gets a few facts. If he had been listening to what was being said he would know I was referring to the Minister of Labour.
Whose estimates will come up later.

The Minister of Labour made remarks about Alberta coal. It was a member of your government, not I, who was saying that it would not stock-pile. If the minister would listen to what is being said instead of being so anxious to rise and "crab" about somebody else, he would hear what is going on.

Let me say this, on a point of order. Let the hon. member discuss this when it comes up on my estimates. I shall still be here, I hope, and any statement my hon. friend has to make I shall do my best to answer. He does not need to fear that the Minister of Labour is going to run away. I thought he was talking about some minister of the gospel.

Don't ever worry. I was talking about you then. On the question of whether this matter should be discussed under this item, in just about a minute I am going to refer to the Minister of Munitions and Supply. When he was giving his statement the other day he occupied about a page under this very item, and he was talking about coal, so that it definitely does come in this place. But this question was raised by myself a year ago in this chamber, as far as western coal is concerned. I was about to state what the Minister of Labour said with regard to the policy of handling it. As reported in Hansard of this year, at page 1057, he had this to say:
I have a vivid recollection of the hon. member for Bow River rising in his place last session and saying that we had no organization to meet a possible shortage of fuel in the west this winter. In the light of what has taken place, I think it can be said that we were not only prepared but overprepared, having regard to weather conditions, to meet the fuel situation in western and eastern Canada this year.
What is wrong with that?
I am just going to tell the minister what is wrong with it. As far as this winter was concerned the minister is perfectly right. He was overprepared; I will agree with him there.
I wonder what my hon. friend would have said if we had not been prepared.
I am coming -to that, too. This winter you were overprepared, so that shows a definite lack of policy.
Or a mild winter.

A year ago you were vastly underprepared. That, too, showed a definite lack of policy. Very likely next year you will be underprepared again. So that it is necessary that a national fuel policy should be gone into carefully and established, and even at this late date it was good news to hear the Minister of Munitions and Supply-the minister, mind you, who says that this does not come under his department-make the statement a few minutes ago that a royal commission is to be set up to investigate this coal situation. It is time it was done, and the Minister of Munitions and Supply, whether it comes under his department or not, is apparently at least moving in the right direction.
Let us see what the Minister of Munitions and Supply, who is so much concerned about the matter being discussed in the wrong

War Appropriation-Supplies

place, had to say about this. The other day, when speaking on his estimates, he said, as
reported in Hansard, at page 1702:
The coal which is mined to-day, and in the next few months, will be marketed for next winter's supply.
That is an appropriate statement. The coal which is mined to-day will be next winter's ' supply. If the minister or whoever is responsible for coal production will follow out his policy on that basis, next year we shall not be in the same position as we were in a year ago and as we are in to-day.
Not if there is an election you won't.

Because surely now is the time, especially when so' many miners all over the country are being laid off, to create a national fuel policy for Canada which will put these men in employment. There is no use in saying, as the Minister of Labour said the other day in regard to the fuel policy, that in a little while some of these soldier miners who are laid off will be taken back to the forces and others will be enlisting in the army.
I never said that.

Yes, the minister did; and that in a little while those miners who came off the farms would be going back to the farms and that that would relieve the unemployment situation. For quite a period men have been walking the streets unemployed. At the time I spoke on this question there were over 700 miners in Drum-heller who had applied for unemployment insurance; a thousand of them did not have any work, and conditions were getting worse. Since then, 500 miners have been laid off in Edmonton. The situation is becoming critical. The Minister of Munitions and Supply, again speaking about coal, had this to say on March 21, as reported in Hansard, at page 1701
By 1943, our consumption had increased to 46 million tons, of which over 28 million tons have been imported.
That amount of coal was imported last year from the United States or Great Britain. He continued:
These figures will give the house some idea of our coal problem. Despite some improvement in the over-all production picture, there is no doubt that we shall have a serious coal problem on our hands for the duration of the war.
Is the time not opportune for the minister's announcement to-day that a royal commission is to be set up? The matter was so serious 'hat I considered I would be negligent in my duty if I did not bring up this question when Mr. Speaker was going to leave the chair for

the house to go into supply, but, the Minister of Munitions and Supply having made the statement that a royal commission is to be set up, I thought that now would be the proper time to discuss the question.
Last year there was an increase over 1942 of 3,243,000 tons of coal which came in from the United States. A subsidy was paid on all that imported coal. Most of it was received by Ontario and Quebec, a market which either Nova Scotia or the western provinces should have for their own. Yet, instead, we are subsidizing all that imported coal, making it still more difficult for our own Canadian mines to keep running, to retain these men in employment, and to hold business within our own country. Some of this coal which was imported and brought to the head of the lakes was taken as far west, on the Canadian Pacific railway, as Saskatchewan, and on the Canadian National Railways, clear into Alberta. Nobody can tell me that that indicates even the semblance of a fuel policy, when in Alberta we have fourteen per cent of the total coal deposits of Canada. Meanwhile mines all over this dominion are being shut down and men are unemployed. I have here a telegram from the board of trade at Drum-heller; I have received also airmail letters from various mines, at Lethbridge, Edmonton and elsewhere. These1 people are greatly concerned over this question. Most of this lack of foresight and judgment, and most of the great unemployment problem that we have been facing could have been and should have been settled long ago if this government had got busy and created a national fuel policy. .
Now a royal commission is going to be set up and I wish to commend the minister. The time is long overdue for it, and if a thorough investigation is made on a national scale I believe that this coal problem can be efficiently and judiciously handled. There is no reason why we cannot keep our miners busy, or begin to prepare now under a proper plan to have these miners put back on the job so as to get coal out now for next winter, and I hope that the government will see to it that every assistance is given the commission, and that after the commission has reported the government will get busy knd set up an efficient national fuel policy for Canada.

I wish to correct a
couple of statements that have been made. It was suggested by the member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) that we had a deliberate policy to force men into the army through these lay-offs that have taken place.

I did not say you had a deliberate policy to force them.

War Appropriation-Supplies

I am glad my hon.
friend admits that. I am satisfied there. I believe I stated the facts clearly this afternoon. The hon. member for Cape Breton South will agree with me, I think, that we did move in the right direction in connection with these lay-offs and the selective service replacements which were undertaken in cooperation with the trades union. This is probably the first time in the history of the country when we have been able to move through the selective service for the purpose of making these changes in such replacements, and that is an indication that we have a machine capable of doing the work. I am proud of it, notwithstanding any opinions to the contrary. We can move, as we have done in many places, people from different jobs to other areas where changes are inevitable.
The grand strategy of the war, as the Minister of Munitions and Supply points out, makes it inevitable that industries will be closed down and others started, and the fact that we have a machine that can move in, as in the case of Dartmouth, and undertake this transfer of workers from one point to another, is an indication that we are a long way ahead of the stage we had reached in the last war.
Let me say to the committee that I am responsible for the call-up of men for military service; and let me say further, very frankly, that with the increase in tempo in the war in Europe there will be greater and greater call-ups of men in the age groups liable for military service. Let there be no mistake about that.
When we see the United States at this very moment considering the cancellation of postponements from eighteen to twenty-six years, whether men are engaged in agriculture or in industry, and when we look at the figures with regard to mobilized -man-power in- Great Britain, it makes our eyes stand out. We have had a staff of industrial engineers and men from the labour department going through the whole industrial structure of the country in the last twelve months with a view to combing out industries in order to meet the requirements of the Department of National Defence.
There may have been in this plant, where we took these 111 -men, such a situation as would have necessitated its shut-down in the not distant future. According to our latest figures, however, there are ample opportunities for employment in the maritime provinces in A, B, C, and D priorities. The latest figures we have for the maritime provinces for total man-power requirements are 12,956; in A and B priorities 9,953 men are required and 1,480 women, making a total of 11,433.
So that my hon. friend will have some indication that, notwithstanding the fact that there are these shifts in the industrial structure, which are inevitable in a time of war, there is ample employment opportunity even in the maritime provinces to take up any slack we may be faced with there. Sometimes there is a temporary closing down and sometimes, necessarily, it is permanent. The same is true of all industries whether in that part of the dominion or in any other section.

I think I had better put the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) straight with regard to the storing of Alberta coal. The minister was quite right when he said that Alberta coal would not store when shipped -here. If you put that coal in a damp cellar it will store for a while, but when it is placed in a dry bin it will not store. I was afraid the hon. member for Bow River might be contemplating using some of the money he makes as a member of parliament for the storing of coal under unfavourable conditions.
Will the hon. member tell us what he means by "store"? Does he mean storing for two years, or for two months, or for how long?

Shipping the coal right here
at this time of the year and putting it in a dry basement. If you do that it will not stand.
For how long?

It will not stand until next
winter. If, however, you put it in a basement where there is a ground floor and a certain amount of dampness, it will store.

It will store for six
months?
If you put it into dry bins at this time of year, by next fall, when you start to draw it out, you will have from five to ten tons of slack per car.

That is
different from what the minister said a moment ago.
Who is right, you or the minister?
I think I ought to know something about it because it cost me money.

The hon. member
should tell us what kind of Alberta coal he is talking about. Alberta -has several kinds.

Drumheller coal. Alberta
coal, which is one of your best.

That is the coal I use and I have no difficulty with it.
War Appropriation-Supplies

We seem to have slipped away from the estimates of munitions and supply into the Department of Labour. There are one or two points arising out of the estimates of munitions and supply which I think should be cleared up by the minister. The first of these points is this: What preparations are being made by his department for the war in the Pacific? Earlier this month the British secretary for war, Sir Jdmes Grigg, speaking in the British House of Commons, used these words:
In one field the ministry (of supply) can expect from us a whole range of new demands -those for specialized weapons and equipment which will be needed when wre transfer our main weight to the war against Japan.
Last fall Admiral Sir Percy Noble, head of the British admiralty delegation at Washington, said there would be a vast expansion of naval base and repair facilities on the British Columbia coast in preparation for the all-out drive against Japan. The policy of the government quite clearly is that once Germany has been disposed of, Canada will throw her whole weight against Japan and that, of course, will require careful preparation by the Department of Munitions and Supply so that the various facilities will be ready when the time comes.
It would be of interest to the committee to hear from the minister just what steps have been taken and what plans he has in mind. I think the bases on the Pacific coast will be main operational bases in the north Pacific when Canada strikes against the Japanese. Probably the shortest route from Great Britain to the Pacific area will be across Canada and through the ports on the Pacific coast. Also there will be great need for ship repair facilities and probably there should be stock piles of equipment built up there even now. Material will be required not only for Canada but also for Australia, New Zealand and the United Kingdom.
It would also seem reasonable that there should be some increased production of war material on that coast, that it would be cheaper and more efficient to have some of the goods manufactured there; more gun barrels, for example, and perhaps different types of guns. When the time comes for Canada to throw her whole weight into the war with Japan it would seem a reasonable thing to do to make more of this equipment on the Pacific coast.
There will also be a great increase in the amount of foodstuffs that will have to be handled through Pacific ports, and in the volume of oil. There was some discussion this afternoon about the Canol project; as the

minister said, that project was undertaken for the express purpose of supplying oil on the Pacific coast. It may be, too, that there will be need for greatly increased warehousing space and for more camps on that coast.
Therefore in many ways preparation should be made, and I would ask the minister to explain just what steps have been taken by his department.
Another question with which I should like the minister to deal is the present policy of the government with regard to shipping. I thought that policy was fairly well defined last year when the minister said on May 12, dealing with Canada's shipping policy:
We expect that the Canadian merchant marine will be a substantial source of employment in the post-war years and that it will be of real benefit to Canadian post-war commerce. That is the policy.
Again last year, the minister made a lengthy speech in Toronto on December 13, and by the way I thought it was a very constructive speech. He had nine suggested objectives for the Canadian people, and objective No. 4 was this:
Canadians should provide a merchant marine worthy of the dominion's export position.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Michaud), nods his head. Tonight he seems to agree with that policy. I hope he has had a change of heart, because on December 24 of last year, after his colleague had given that splendid objective to the Canadian people the Minister of Transport-and by the way, he is the man who would have to administer the shipping policy for Canada-
He will not be there then.

If the government were there. He used these words, and they are serious for those of us who are interested in shipping. They are serious because they are really defeatist. So that I hope the Minister of Transport has changed his mind and that when he used these words he was not stating the policy of the government. He said this:
I see no future in Canada going into the shipping business on a big scale after the war. Some of the ships might well be used to develop-trade between Canada and the West Indies and. South America.
That is the smaller ships, I presume. He went on:
But to enter competition for trade across the Atlantic and Pacific would be a big undertaking.
The Minister of Transport is nodding his head again. I do not know now whether he is with me or against me. I thought he was with me a few minutes ago. At all events, I say

War Appropriation-Supplies
that is a defeatist policy for Canada, and I suggest to the Minister of Munitions and Supply that he make an announcement tonight, or if he does not wish to do it to-night, then to-morrow, as to what Canada's shipping policy is to be.
When he was speaking of his department the other day he said that Canada's merchant navy at the end of February, 1944, comprised fifty-four 10,000-ton ships, of which ten were tankers, and thirteen 4,700-ton ships, making a total of sixty-seven, all built by ourselves in our, own yards and by our own workmen. Then he said that by the end of August of this year we would have thirty additional 10,000-ton ships, of which three would be tankers. That would give us at the end of August ninety-seven ships, less whatever number happened to be sunk in the meantime. In addition, we have an unknown number of ships which have been lent or turned over to the British government, but which are to be returned after the war. I would ask the minister, when he replies, to tell us how many ships Canada has on loan to the British.
We have built up a great corps of merchant seamen. Canada at War, No. 33, February, 1944, showed that there were then certified in the central registry at Ottawa 44,498 Canadian merchant seamen. So that we have approximately 45,000 merchant seamen, and we have great facilities for training merchant seamen- men for the engine rooms, men for the decks-and also facilities, I think, for training officers. We have a plan for operating these ships under a crown company known as Park Steamships Limited, which turns the ships over to the different shipping firms under agreements which provide for the payment of a fee for operating them.
So that Canada is now in a position to have after the war a fine merchant navy; a merchant navy, as the minister said in his speech at Toronto in December, that is worthy of our export position. I would ask him to-night to tell the committee the government policy with regard to the merchant navy and, if he can, to tell us what the plan is for operating that merchant navy, and for allotting the ships between the two coasts. To date the allotment has been fair I think, about fifty-fifty, half to the east coast and half to the Pacific.
Perhaps the minister would also tell us at the same time whether Canada has decided to build faster merchant ships. Some of us raised that point last year and suggested that it might be wise for Canada to have some faster ships. So far, we have been building ships with a speed of ten or eleven knots, while the British and Americans are building ships
which go about fifteen knots. The minister said on June 11 of last year, dealing with this point:
From the Canadian standpoint the building of faster ships is a post-war rather than a present-day war problem, for which the necessary advice is now being secured from the best sources.
There seems to be a great deal of uncertainty as to whether this is the wise course. The war expenditures committee reported on this question of the type of ships that should be built. It said, and this appears in Votes and Proceedings of January 26, 1944;
We suggest, however, that efforts should be made to ascertain if construction of such a ship-
That is a faster ship:
-for post-war use is practicable in Canada with a view to keeping as many yards as possible occupied to meet expected commercial requirements.
There is a great deal of doubt in the United States as to the value of the slow ships in post-war trade. I have here a newspaper report with regard to these 10,000-ton ships in the United States. They are called Liberty ships, which is the American equivalent of the slow ship we are building. It says:
The remainder will be Liberty type ships, which experts says are not suitable for post-war carrying trade.
So that there does seem to be some doubt whether they will be of much use after the war. In view of the fact that Canada exports largely primary products in bulk, I think many of these slow ships could be used by us. I suggest, however, that some attempt should be made to build the faster ships in Canada.
I would ask the minister to tell us something with regard to the two questions I have raised: first of all, as to the preparations that are being made for Canada to take part in the war in the Pacific; and, second, with regard to Canada's shipping policy as it stands at the present time.

In reply to the first question I would remind my hon. friend that the Department of Munitions and Supply does not set the requirements; they are set out by the chiefs of staff. However, the department is doing certain specialized work in connection with the war in the Pacific, in the nature of maintenance ships and victualling ships, definitely for the Pacific; certain landing craft, definitely for the Pacific, and certain types of weapons definitely for the Pacific war. In the matter of overhaul facilities, these are being strengthened gradually and will be kept ahead of requirements, as far as repair work
1S94
War Appropriation-Supplies

on the Pacific is concerned. We are in excellent position, I think, to handle repair work there; we have good drydock capacity and good berthing space for repairs. Just as we have looked after the requirements for the war in the Atlantic, I think we shall be able to look after the requirements of the army, the navy and the air force for the war in the Pacific.
Before the minister leaves that point, will there be any extension of the production of war equipment on the coast? Is that in mind?

No; I would not think so. If we had a factory in Montreal or Toronto producing materials for the Pacific, I am sure my hon. friend would not suggest that we abandon that factory and start a new one on the west coast. I doubt if the level of production on the Pacific coast will increase greatly on account of the war in the Pacific. We have an excellent production machine in full gear which will probably supply the equipment. In ship repairs and perhaps shipbuilding there may be a step-up on that account; and there may be greater activity in the movement of troops.
What about storage room, warehouse room?

We are not in bad shape; we are always building a bit more warehouse space there, and I suppose that will continue. As far as the merchant fleet is concerned, as my hon. friend says the Canadian fleet at the moment includes sixty-nine new ships, and thirty more will be added during the current year. The hon. gentleman asked for the number that have been delivered to Britain. That number stands at eighty-eight at the moment, and additional ships will be built for operation by the United Kingdom during the coming year.
Mr. GREEN; Those are all returnable to Canada after the war, are they?
Yes. In addition, we have sold ninety ships to the maritime commission for cash. Of course those have passed out of our possession.
That is to the United States?

Yes. In the early days of the war we sold two ships to Britain for cash, and we have also lent one ship to Australia. The policy of the government is, I think, the same as the policy being followed in the United States and the United Kingdom. The routes for the ships and the trades to be served are determined by a shipping board.

The Canadian shipping board determines the services which these boats shall perform. Actually the boats are managed by established operating companies, for a fee. All the earnings of the boats are returnable to the government through Park Steamship company Those earnings are substantial; I notice that Park Steamship company already has turned over to the receiver general some 810,000,000 of earnings from those ships. We expect that at the end of the war, as far as the Canadian fleet is concerned, the cost of the boats will be written down considerably. Possibiy some will be fully paid for, which will put the fleet in a strong position for the post-war years.
There is a tendency, and I think an undue tendency, to belittle the type of tonnage that makes up the Canadian merchant marine. The ships that we have built have been progressively improved since we started, and are all first-class tramp tonnage, better than any tramp tonnage that existed before the war. I think every practical shipping man will agree that they are the best design for boats of their class that anyone knows of at this time. They are the type of boat that has always carried eighty-five per cent of Canada's export trade. There is a need, based on pre-war business, for about 150 of these ships, to move exports from the west coast to their markets, and we hope that post-war levels will require an even larger number of these ships. I am happy to say that we shall be able to supply ships of Canadian ownership for these trades.
Did the minister say 150 ships from the west coast alone?

Yes. Similarly, based on prewar movements, seventy-five ships will be required for export movement from the east coast, for bulk commodities. I think at the end of the war our fleet will be sufficient to take care of both requirements. The cargo that goes into boats of this class is of the type that is handled as freight on our railroads. Express shipments ordinarily would go in faster tonnage. As far as this country is concerned, tramp tonnage in the past has not required subsidy, whereas every boat of the express type has required an operating subsidy from the Canadian government. Further, it is a fact that the high speed boats and express service boats are built for special trades and special operations. They are not boats that can be built under conditions of mass production with any probability that they would suit the requirements of the trade for which they were designed. Therefore it seems to us and to our expert advisers that it is not wise at this time to attempt to go

War Appropriation-Supplies
into the passenger steamship building or the fast freighter building in a big way. We hope the efficiency of our yards will be such that at the end of the war we shall have requests from operators of liner services to build their ships in Canada.
That is passenger boats, as well as fast freighters?

We will welcome that business and do all we can to encourage it. But as far as the present building programme is concerned, we are building a ship that we know Canada will need, ships that will stand on their merits, ships that will be the backbone of any post-war merchant fleet that Canada will require. Does that cover the point?

There is great concern as to whether or not the shipbuilding industry will be able to survive after the war. As the minister knows, after the last war the shipbuilding industry collapsed, and in the back of everyone's mind there is the feeling that the same thing may happen after this war. I am delighted indeed to hear the minister say tonight that the plan is to increase our merchant fleet, and that apparently it is the intention of the government to maintain a Canadian merchant navy. But can he give any assurance to the Canadian people that the Canadian government is determined to maintain the * shipbuilding industry after the war? I realize that it could not be on anything like the scale of to-day, but I do hope some definite word can go out to the country that the government intends to see to it that our shipbuilding industry is maintained. Perhaps it would be necessary to subsidize the building of ships; in the United States they have long since decided that this was a wise policy. It might be possible to keep the industry up by government orders. The minister knows, just as I do, and other members of the committee, that it will be a difficult problem to keep the shipbuilding industry going steadily after the war. Yet it does seem to' be one of those industries of which Canada has the greatest need. I think it should definitely be a government policy that we are determined to have a shipbuilding industry, even if in the beginning it cost money. Can the minister go so far as to say that it is the intention of the government to foster shipbuilding in Canada in the post-war years, or, in other words, that steps will be taken to see to it that the industry does not shrivel up, once the war is over.

I have always understood my hon. friend to be a great exponent of free enterprise. I can point out to him that we have established in Canada a first-class shipbuilding industry, with extensive facilities that will be written off during the war period. Ours will be low-cost yards, so far as overhead goes. Ours will be efficient yards. Our shipbuilding costs are very satisfactory, and they have been coming down steadily.
What are they now? What is the cost of one of these ships?
I delivered an oration on that subject this afternoon, stating that I do not give costs. I am sorry my hon. friend was absent.
Oh, I was here.
It did not register, then.

Mr. H. R. MacMillan, formerly head of Wartime Merchant Shipping, gave certain figures in Vancouver on January 13. He said that these ships were turned out at from 81,300,000 to $1,500,000 each, as compared with $900,000 in British yards and $2,000,000 in the United States. And, considering everything, he regarded this an excellent showing for Canada.
Mr. HOWE That is not far off. The Canadian position is a little better than that now since each ship costs a little less than the preceding one. Yards that were out of line in the matter of cost are coming into line. We have a very good showing from our shipyards at the present time. Naturally, for the reasons I gave this afternoon, the larger yards build ships more cheaply than do the smaller ones, and the older yards usually do better than the new ones. However, the difference is not great.
Some of them are very efficient.

Yes; there are some very
efficient yards in Canada. Our shipbuilders will be in an excellent position to compete. We have taken steps to improve the competitive position. We have brought into Canada a very strong designing firm, so that if anyone comes to Canada wanting a ship for any particular service, and can give us the requirements, the ship can be designed here in an efficient manner.

Does that include passenger
ships?

Yes. And we have taken such steps as we can at this stage to place our shipyards in a strong position, so that they may compete. I sincerely hope and believe that a policy of subsidies will not be necessary. I think an aggressive policy of salesmanship will keep our yards busy. I know that at this
War Appropriation-Supplies

time, if the yards were not occupied in war work they would be able to take on a good deal of private work. They have not been able to take such work, on account of the requirements of war. My hon. friend would not ask me to go farther than that, but I hope if he comes into office he will not immediately jump into the business of subsidies.

I agree with the minister;
it would be far better if subsidies were not necessary. But I said it might come to that stage, rather than let the industry die out.

That, I understand, is a
philosophy of despair. I prefer to be hopeful.

Do the minister's
remarks apply to great lakes points, as well?

Great lakes yards are busy at the present time, and are likely to be busy for some considerable time. The type of boat which can be built on the lakes is restricted, either to tonnage for the great lakes, or to tonnage which can pass through the St. Lawrence canals. There is every indication that there will be business for great lakes yards for some considerable time.

I should like to ask
the minister about another matter. Two years ago he discussed at some length the Pogue carburettor. Might I point out to him that another carburettor has been patented by the editor of one of the newspapers in my constituency. I know this public-spirited citizen very well, and I understand he has offered the Department of Munitions and Supply the opportunity to use his discovery. I find that the rural municipality has passed a resolution urging that this gasoline saver, which has been tested and is reported to have done 130 miles to a gallon, should be investigated. In view of the fact that this department is spending over $8,000,000 a day of the people's money, the very small amount of money involved in testing this carburettor would be insignificant.
I believe that some day some person will discover a carburettor which is an improvement on any at present on the market, and there is no reason why the editor of a newspaper in a small country town, a man with a creative mind, and one who has been willing to spend a considerable sum of money, many hours of time and to use a large amount of material, should not discover something of importance. Would the minister make a statement as to the policy of his department? Is it interested in spending small sums of money in testing inventions of this kind?
I understand that Mr. Augustus, who is the editor, and his partner Mr. Melnyk, have offered this invention as a service to the

country. They have suggested that if it is of any use the government should pay them how it likes, when it likes and if it likes. Nothing would appear to be fairer, and I should imagine it would be sound policy for the minister's department to test this invention, and satisfy the people in that community as to whether it has or has not any merit.

The policy of the government toward inventions is liberal and advanced. We have a board known as the dominion inventions board, composed of the best scientists in Canada. All my hon. friend needs do is to submit his carburettor to that board, and if the board reports that the invention has promise, he will find large sums of money available for its development. If, on the other hand, the board reports unfavourably, he can do what he likes with his invention, but he can get no help from any department of government in connection with it.
That is fair enough; but my information is that the inventor has offered it to the department, and that nothing has happened.

It is quite useless for your friends to offer it to my department; they must offer it to the inventions board. If the board decides that the invention has merit, , my, department will then be very much interested in it. But until then we have no interest whatsoever in the invention.

I think the minister's department might show the courtesy of writing the inventor, suggesting what action should be taken, or that it should turn the letter over. My complaint is that he did not receive any information from the department.
Undoubtedly the letter has automatically been handed to the inventions board. All letters of that kind are handled in that way.

I should like to say a word about carburettors. A couple of years ago I spoke on several occasions respecting the Pogue carburettor. But, so far as I know, nothing has come of it- although I think the government did spend some money in experiments. May I suggest that this government is not giving enough encouragement to people who have invented carburettors, to see whether or not there is any merit in those inventions.
I know the minister may be irritated at times because a great number of persons come in to him with the information that they have inventions respecting new types of carburettors which will do this or do that. The tendency is to brush them aside, and to put

War Appropriation-Supplies
the onus on them to prove the value of their invention. In my opinion that is not the proper procedure.
Let me tell the committee about an experience I had in this city. Almost a year ago a man who lives here in Ottawa came into my office in this building with an attachment to put on a carburettor. He told, me that he was not trying to sell it and that he did not care whether the government used it or whether I used it, but he told me that his experience had been that this attachment would increase the efficiency of the carburettor by twenty to thirty per cent. He gave me this thing and I took it home. I did not brush off the idea lightly; I put it on my car. I did not have all the mechanical things with which to test it, but I filled up my car and drove a hundred miles and I found that this attachment raised the gasoline mileage from twenty to twenty-seven miles a gallon. My car was a 1941 Chevrolet. I was not satisfied with the one test; I tried another and I found it did the same thing.
I would not give that to any government.

Probably you would not give it any consideration. That attachment increased the efficiency by twenty to thirty per cent. I venture to say that it would not cost the government more than three cents apiece to make these things. I brought up this matter before because I was much concerned about it. If the government is not concerned in saving twenty-five or thirty per cent of our gasoline, why should anyone else be? If the government wants it, I am ready to give them all the information I have. I will not go any farther than that because I am not concerned with it. I would think that when we are so urgently in need of gasoline it would be worth while to investigate some of these things.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Was it sent to the inventions board?
Not that I know of.

There is a matter I should like to bring up which is somewhat different from the other questions that have been raised. I refer to the use of daylight saving time. When the regulations putting this time into effect were brought in back in 1939 or 1940. the minister pointed out that this action was being taken because of the necessity of conserving electricity. Many people throughout Canada, particularly those in the country districts, feel that we Should go back to ordinary time, especially in the winter time.
It has been found extremely difficult to get children off to school in the dark. When one looks around the city of Ottawa and other cities during the winter time it is hard to see where any real, saving has been achieved by the enforcement of daylight saving time, because in most buildings, and in this one too, all the lights burn throughout the entire day. I wonder if the introduction of daylight saving has brought about the saving in electricity that was expected. Has any consideration been given to going back to regular time?

Consideration is being given from time to time to requests similar to the one being made now by the hon. member. It might be worth while to tell hon. members what the effect would be. In the maritime provinces it is estimated that the demand for power would be increased by approximately ten per cent if standard time were restored. The existing generating facilities are already heavily loaded and the reserve capacity is barely adequate for present requirements. An increase of approximately ten per cent in the maximum demand would be undersirable at the present time.
In the province of Quebec the demand for power in the metropolitan areas would be increased by over 60,000 horse-power. The reserve generating capacity at present available to the interconnected power systems is not sufficient to permit the absorption of such a large additional demand with safety.
In Ontario the demand for power would be increased by over 75,000 horse-power. At the present time Ontario is short of peak power. An additional demand of 75,000 horse-power would be unfortunate at this time and during certain hours would require reductions of power now being delivered.
In the prairie provinces the power systems have for the most part sufficient generating capacity to carry the increased demand without inconvenience. In British Columbia the demand for power in the Vancouver district would be increased by approximately 13,000 horse-power. The generating stations in the district are already heavily loaded. If the demand should be increased by 13,000 horsepower the amount of power required at times of maximum use would exceed the combined capacity of the available hydro plants and the reliability of service would be endangered. The prairies would appear to be the only area that could go back to old time as far as the power situation is concerned.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to complete the remarks I was making this afternoon when I was pointing out the
War Appropriation-[DOT]Supplies

ways in which government policy in connection with the synthetic rubber plant at Sarnia is concentrating power in the hands of a few private companies. I referred to the manner in which private companies have been called in to operate this government-owned plant and also to the fact that enlargements of private rubber plants were being financed by the government. I referred to the large orders which have had to be given to these companies. The point I was making was that public funds are being used to strengthen the position of a few private companies in the rubber industry. And yet, after the war, the consuming public when purchasing rubber goods will have to pay prices that will provide profits to these private companies despite the fact that the stronger position of these companies has been brought about by the use of public funds which were made available to them in the interests of the war effort.
This recognition of the problem created by the concentration of power in the hands of a few companies is to be found not only in this group, but also in other quarters. I should like to quote from page 31 of Saturday Night of March 18, 1944, as follows:
lo an extent as yet undetermined the concentration of industrial capacity has been increased by reason of the unavoidable reliance placed upon large producers in securing war supplies in the shortest possible time.
That is a very good statement of what has actually taken place. If I may quote further:
This fact must be faced so that we may begin to think of the means which must be developed to ensure that those producers who will hold a monopoly or quasi-monopoly position in the post-war period will make full use of the productive capacity which they will control, and not endeavour to maximize profits by curtailing output or maintaining prices at high levels.
I have given that quotation to indicate that others, like those in this group, are worried about the problem created by this concentration of power in the hands of a small number of private corporations. Hon. members will readily recognize that we do not feel that the proposals suggested in the quotation which I have read will meet the problem. Our view' is that when power has been concentrated there is only one place to put it in order to make sure that it will not be used against the public good. The place to put that concentration of power is in the hands of the people themselves.
I should like to take a moment to read briefly from an address given in Washington, D.C., on February 12, 1943, by Wendell Berge, assistant attorney general of the United States. The subject of his address was in the form of a question, "What shall we do about 
cartels in the post-war period?" I consider that his statement with respect to cartels applies to monopolies in general, and that the points he made are points which indicate what may be the outgrowth of the policy being pursued by the government at the present time. I quote from Mr. Berge:
In general, cartels restrict rather than promote _ trade. Cartels typically engage in such practices as dividing fields of operation and market areas between members so as to eliminate competition, restricting production by agreement, and fixing prices so as to avoid price competition. They also promote various kinds of patent licensing contracts which enable them to control and limit the use of new inventions and thus restrict the benefits of technological advance. The effects of these practices include reduced production and employment, higher prices and profits, retarded spread of technological improvements and a lower standard of living.
It is this sort of thing which-frankly-we are afraid of in the post-war period, because of the kind of concentration which has been made necessary by the "unavoidable reliance placed upon large producers for the procurement of war supplies in the shortest possible time." That, indeed, is the reason we have called attention to government policy with respect to the Aluminum Company of Canada, Canadian Industries Limited, Canadian Pacific Air Lines, and, now, the situation with respect to rubber. As I said a few days ago, we are pleased that the government has realized what a private corporation such as the Canadian Pacific is able to do in a short space of time when it is given unlimited opportunity and a free hand. We are glad that the government has decided to take certain steps even though they may not go far enough, in connection with that problem. We feel that this question of rubber calls for the same kind of approach. Our position is that when, under the necessities of war, power has to be concentrated as it is, the people of this country and the government must think in terms of extending the principle of public ownership. That is the only way by which one can make sure that the benefits of modern science and of technological development will accrue to the people as a whole. That is our concern. We feel that we have had an expression of that principle in the period of war. It has been necessary to get goods produced to wage the conflict in which we are engaged, and to the extent that those goods are produced and used for our common defence they are being used for the benefit of the people as a whole. In that sense the benefit of the accelerated war-time production and technological improvements accrues fo the people. We want to make sure that these benefits will likewise

accrue to the people of Canada as a whole, not to private corporations or private finance, when the war is over. Therefore, I urge that the house and the country face the fact that, as economic power becomes concentrated, there is only one place to put it so as to be sure that it will be used for the benefit of the people, and that is in the hands of the people themselves. That is our position. We in this group believe that it is the only answer to one of the greatest problems which has been created during the present war.

May I make a few remarks in reply. My hon. friend, I think, has been preparing a speech for the hustings. He cannot be serious about what has happened and what has been done at Polymer.
Polymer is a plant owned by the people of Canada. It is a public ownership plant. I have a good deal of experience with public ownership and with private ownership. I have been an industrial engineer in this country for practically thirty-five years. I have worked almost continuously for governments and for private interests, both. Perhaps I have carried out .more work measured in dollar value for private interests, but I have worked for every government in this country during every year, beginning in 1912.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We might give you a job, too.

Public interests are just as
capable of building a plant as private interests. The whole test is in the operating.
Exactly.

If we could guarantee that
governments could operate plants as efficiently as private interests there would be a very good argument that public ownership is better than private ownership. That could be argued. The difficulty is this: if a private industry is not well managed-and plenty are not-it will go broke in a short time, be reorganized, and put under more efficient management. Under public operation that usually does not happen.
Hear, hear.

It goes steadily down grade.
It is allowed to go down grade, unless it becomes enough of a scandal, when the government is very apt to get rid of it and pass it to private hands.

Like the Canadian
National Railways!

I have started a good many
public operations during this war. In every case I have tried to put them under efficient management, the management will make them a public enterprise to serve the country well.
My hon. friend is quite wrong about Polymer. The Polymer corporation is operated by a board of directors, men placed there by the government to have an over-all supervision of the business operation of the plant. The board of Polymer recommend to the government the contracts to be made for the purchase of raw materials, and they have full responsibility in advising the government as to the distribution of the product and as to the price. There are certain very involved technical processes in the plant which are divided into three parts: the butadiene production, which is operated by a subsidiary of Imperial Oil; the styrene process, which. is operated by a Canadian subsidiary of the Dow Chemical company; and the polymerization plant, which is operated by a company organized by the four rubber companies which have research laboratories in Canada, as well as a complete knowledge of the kind of rubber required by Canadian industry. Why is that so? The reason why Imperial Oil were asked to organize the management of the butadiene end is that Imperial have a very large research staff, a trained organization in that special line of production. It was felt that their management would be progressive; that if improvements were brought into the industry they would be put into the polymer plant; and we would be sure at all times of a modern and efficient operation of the butadiene end. It might be asked, why not pick two or three men from the Imperial organization, hire them and put them in charge? It requires more than the knowledge of one or two men; it calls for the knowledge of a strong organization backed by a research laboratory and by trained research chemists *who will advance the art and apply the advancement of industry to the process they have in hand for polymer.
St. Clare Processing company receive a fee for their scientific management of that particular operation. They have nothing whatever to do with the cost of the product at any stage. They simply have a process to manage, and their duty is to carry out that duty as efficiently as possible. The same applies to the Dow Chemical company, which invented the process for the production of styrene. That company is by far the largest producer of styrene on the continent, and the only company that has full knowledge of the art of that particular production. There again we know we have a management that will be as good as any that can be obtained anywhere and that our process will not be allowed to be outmoded. We shall always be up to date on that process.
As regards the polymerization end, we are making rubber to be used by the Canadian
War Appropriation-Supplies

trade. We want to make the kind of rubber that the trade can use for the purpose of making tires and other finished products which the Canadian people will require. Naturally, we choose the operators of that process from among men who know the requirements of the trade, who know what rubber is and what grades of rubber are required for different products. Here again, these men have nothing to do with the distribution of rubber. They simply make rubber of the required grades, and after it is manufactured it is priced and distributed by the directors of the Polymer Corporation or by such agencies as the government may appoint for the purpose.
It is absurd to say that any one of these men profits unduly by the operation or gets any advantage over competitors. It is just as important to the smallest rubber user in the country to have the quality of rubber from polymer suitable to his needs as it is to the largest company, and the people of Canada as a whole will benefit from polymer only as the product is made cheaply and of the best possible quality.
I hope my hon. friend will refrain from using the line of argument he did to-day. I think it is a little beneath him. The only danger to public ownership is that my hon. friend might get into a position of responsibility and allow his prejudices against certain large firms and against combines and cartels, to interfere with his obligations to keep the management of these great plants, built at government expense, in an efficient state. That is the real menace to government ownership.

Present: His Excellency the Governor General in Council: Whereas the Minister oif Munitions and Supply reports that substantial stocks of surplus assets, the property of the government oi Canada are currently being created as a result of changes from time to time in war production programmes, the progress of the waT, the development of new types of equipment and other factors; That it is desirable and in the public interest that surplus assets owned by the government should be dealt with in such manner as to cause the minimum of dislocation of the economic structure of the country so as to assist in the orderly transition to a peacetime basis of production, following the cessation of hostilities, of industries which during the war period have been wholly or substantially engaged in production for war purposes; and That in his opinion, a suitable mode of procedure, to meet the current situation, would 'be: (a) 'for the governor in council to direct, that each government department or agency should survey and investigate all lands, buildings, structures, plant, machinery, equipment, articles and things (including munitions of war and supplies as defined in The Department of Munitions and Supply Act), and any interests therein or parts thereof, which are held or administered by it, with a view to the determination of the types and quantities of such assets which are surplus to the needs of such department or agency;	(b)	to constitute an inter-departmental committee which will be charged with the duty of obtaining reports from government departments and agencies with respect to such surpluses and of receiving and dealing with applications from any department or agency for any assets which are surplus to the needs of the department or agency bolding or administering such assets, and of formulating and recommending general policies with respect to the disposal of assets which are surplus to the needs of the government;
