(d)	to create a company which will act as the agent of the government and will be charged with the duty of disposing of or otherwise dealing with surplus assets from time to time transferred or consigned to it and of making recommendations on matters of policy and courses of action with respect to such surplus assets or which in the opinion of the company will promote the national well-being of Canada. Therefore, His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Munitions and Supply and under and by virtue of the powers conferred by the War Measures Act, the Department of Munitions and Supply Act, and the War Appropriation Act No. 2, 1942, is pleased to make and doth hereby make the following order: Order 1.	The term "surplus crown assets" where used in this order means any land, buildings, structures, plant, machinery, equipment, scrap, materials, articles or things, or any interest therein or any part thereof, and all munitions of war and supplies as defined by the Department of Munitions and Supply Act, which are owned or controlled by the government of Canada or any agency thereof and which for the time being, or from time to time, are surplus to the current or probable future requirements of the war programme of Canada or the needs of the government of Canada or any agency thereof. 2.	It shall be the duty of each government department and agency from time to time to survey and investigate all lands, buildings, structures, plant, machinery, equipment, munitions of war and supplies, scrap, materials, articles and things, and any interests therein or parts thereof, from time to time on hand in or administered by such department or agency and to report from time to time to the allocation committee hereinafter mentioned the assets which are or are likely to become surplus to the needs of such department or agency. 3.	There is hereby established under the Minister of Munitions and Supply, or such other minister as may be hereafter designated by the governor in council (hereinafter referred to as "the minister"), an interdepartmental committee, to be known as the "crown assets allocation committee" (hereinafter referred to as the "allocation committee") having the powers and duties hereinafter set forth.

There is a little information I have been waiting to ask the minister for. He made a reference to the destroyer programme; he referred to one having been launched and said that the turbine units will be installed this summer, boilers having been installed. Would he tell the committee to what extent the armament, boilers and fittings of various descriptions including the machinery are Canadian made? Will the destroyers be Canadian-built from hull to topmast?

The purpose of undertaking the building of destroyers in Canada was to develop the art of building destroyers here. The intention was that they should be Canadian built in every particular. We have gone into the building of the type of turbines used in destroyers, we have developed engines for them, and we are developing every item of a destroyer. The purpose is also to be able to make repairs here and to increase the fleet. We did it knowing that the cost would be higher than the cost of building the same ships in England. We think the cost is not going to be tremendously" higher. The first ship always costs more than repetitive ships. We estimated that the time required would be about one year longer than in the old country, but the indications are that it will not be as much as that-perhaps eight months longer than the Tribals we have had built in the United Kingdom during the war. We are developing the art of building destroyers in this country. As my hon. friend knows very well, a destroyer is a complicated ship. It is more difficult to build than a cruiser, which is a larger ship but less intricate in its arrangements. I think we are introducing a valuable type of knowledge that will be very useful in our future development.
Does that cover armament as well?

Yes. I think the biggest gun on a destroyer is a 4-7-inch and we are making 4-7-inch guns here. If we are not, we are capable of making them. I am not sure, but I think I am correct in saying that all the armament is made here.

Has the government or the minister's department established as yet a policy in reference to the disposal of singlepurpose machinery? A great deal of the equipment that has been used in the production of war munitions is single-purpose machinery, heavy castiron machines. I have observed in more than one place a considerable quantity of single-purpose machines stored up, made largely of castiron, and many of them very heavy. I have wondered on more than one occasion whether it would not be advisable just to smash them up and use them as castiron. They never, can be used for any other work than what they were made for. It 'would be uneconomic to try to make anything else with them, and there is not much else that they could make. Since there appears to be a surplus of these machines I have felt that it would be much better to order them smashed up and melted down to make other machines. Has any policy been suggested or established by the board for the disposal of all such single-purpose machines?

A policy has been established for the sale of government machines. A floor price has been established below which they cannot be sold. Quite a number of machines have been surrendered to War Assets Corporation for sale. As a matter of fact, sales of machines are constantly taking place. So far as single-purpose machines are concerned, some have a future and some have not. The corporation is charged with the responsibility of recommending to the government the destruction of machines if a market cannot be found for them. They cannot be sold below a certain base price; in other words, they 100-120
are not thrown on the bargain counter. If they are not worth the base price they will be reduced to scrap and returned to the smelter.

Take a shell machine, for example. I remember very well that following the last war large numbers of shell machines were sledge-hammered and smashed into scrap iron. At the time the price of scrap iron went very low, and the same thing might happen after this war. If either the department or the board determines that so many hundred or so many thousand of these machines cannot be used for any other purpose after the war, would it not be more advantageous to take that surplus and order it destroyed while scrapiron prices are high, so that the scrap may be used to make something required in the prosecution of the war?

Of course it is a bit early to talk about scrapping single-purpose machines now. The demand for shells may increase and the machines may be required for that single purpose. I can assure my hon. friend, however, that no great accumulation of machines will be permitted, but that there will be a sorting out as between those that can be destroyed and those that cannot.

I should like to ask one or two other questions in regard to this synthetic rubber proposition. I do not think the minister really did himself justice in the differentiation he made between public and private ownership of industry; I believe he said a government could erect a factory but it could not always operate one as efficiently as private industry. As a member of the cabinet the minister has had supervision in turn over the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and Trans-Canada Air Lines which, if one may take at face value his speech of the other day, intends to broaden rather than constrict its field of public ownership. So that I do not think the minister was on particularly good ground in advancing the argument that a government could not efficiently operate-
I did not say it could not; I said the test was whether it could or not.

That is the test; and where it has been given a fair trial it seems to me the minister himself is one of the men who have been largely responsible for some very efficient administration of government owned enterprises.
I wonder if the minister could explain the set-up with reference to Polymer and its relations with Imperial Oil and Dow Chemical

War Appropriation-Supplies

Just what is the situation, and what will be the situation after the war? As I understand it, Imperial Oil are manufacturing butadiene from petroleum, and for that purpose they have a pipeline running into Sarnia. In the event of the government deciding to continue the manufacture of synthetic rubber after the war, or in the event of the government deciding to sell Polymer, what would be the position of Imperial Oil? Would the fact that they have this oil-line put them in a preferred position? Would they be in the position that since they have the only pipeline supplying the petroleum out of which they make butadiene, they alone could buy the assets of Polymer, or they alone could supply or refuse to supply any other company that bought the synthetic rubber plant at Sarnia? It Beems to me the fear that is in the mind of many of us, and that the minister could help to clear up, though he has not done so yet, is that the Canadian people have put $4S,000,000 into a splendid piece of engineering, but at the same time Imperial Oil, because of their preferred position, because they have a pipeline in there and because of the fact that they will be supplying the butadiene gas to make the synthetic rubber, will be in a preferred position after the war and will have a controlling voice in the industry.
Then the minister said that this Polymer plant is operating for the good of the Canadian people and for the good of all the rubber companies, large and small. Could the minister give the committee some information as to how buna-S, which I understand is the term for the crude rubber, has been distributed as between the different rubber companies in Canada of which, if I am correctly informed, there are some fifty or sixty? Just how has it been distributed; how have the small companies benefited as compared with the larger companies? As my colleague pointed out this afternoon, the president of Polymer is the general manager of Goodyear Tire and Rubber; the assistant rubber controller is vicepresident of the Dominion Rubber company, and so far as we know these men still have their business connections. Does that mean these rubber companies are in a preferred position? Are they in a position to get a larger share of the raw rubber than are the smaller . companies which are not so fortunately situated?
The third question I wanted to ask the minister was in reference to a statement he made the other day, I think in answer to the hon. member for North Battleford. He compared the cost of producing alcohol from grain and from petroleum, and he said that producing it from grain cost about three and a
fMr. T. C. Douglas.]
half times as much. As I understand it, when the synthetic rubber plant at Sarnia was getting under way, in the initial stages they did produce synthetic rubber from grain alcohol until they got the more elaborate process set up for producing butadiene from petroleum. Would the minister have any figures, not as to the cost of producing grain alcohol, but as to the cost of the finished synthetic rubber produced from grain alcohol as compared with synthetic rubber produced from petroleum? The reason why I ask that question is that I think the minister has given the figure for producing grain alcohol, but he has not given it for the rubber. I have been surprised to find the extent to which grain alcohol is being produced in the United States, and apparently produced economically. In the Montreal Gazette of March 24 of this year I see the following news item:
Washington, March 23. The United States war production board has under consideration twenty-eight proposals for expanded production of industrial alcohol, a senate agriculture subcommittee was advised to-day.
Doctor Walter G. Whitman, assistant director of the board's chemicals bureau, submitted details of the proposals, including type of alcohol to be produced, company and location, anticipated annual production and total estimated costs.
The alcohol would be produced from several sources-petroleum, sulphite liquor, wood waste, grains, sweet potatoes and other materials.
Then it goes on:
Grain proposals outnumber all others, with twelve in all.
In other words, some twelve out of the twenty-eight dealt with the manufacture of alcohol from grain. Then the article proceeds to give the list of plants, the cost of erecting them, and their location, which I do not think is of interest to the committee. The point is that in the United States out of twenty-eight plants they propose to erect twelve for the production of alcohol from grain; and it seems to me that if they can do so economically in the United States, and if they find it beneficial to do so, the minister has not given a satisfactory explanation as to why alcohol cannot be produced from grain in western Canada; not on the basis of $1.40, but produced in western Canada where low-grade wheat can be bought on the prairies for a much lower figure. I would ask the minister those three questions.

In asking his first question
about the preferred position of Imperial Oil, my hon. friend is quite mistaken when he says that Imperial Oil sells butadiene to the Polymer corporation. Imperial Oil sells petroleum to the Polymer corporation. It is made into butadiene in the Polymer plant, the technical

War Appropriation-Supplies
management of which is under a subsidiary of Imperial Oil. But it is decidedly separate; the operation is for and on account of, and with equipment owned by the Polymer
corporation.

Let me get
that straight. The minister means that the petroleum is turned into butadiene by a subsidiary of Imperial, working on a management-fee basis?
Yes; that is correct.
And it is produced by Imperial Oil?

No; it is not produced by
Imperial Oil; it is produced by the Polymer corporation. If I manage a plant, I do not produce it; the plant produces it.
The personnel are of Imperial Oil.

The personnel is, yes. The
personnel are Polymer, managed by Imperial
Oil.	But supposing the government owns the Ottawa Car and Foundry; they place a management contract with myself, personally, to manage that plant. The plant is still owned by the crown, and the product is still that of the crown. I simply handle the mechanics, and turn out the product. And that applies at Sarnia. What I am saying is that we have no business dealings with Imperial Oil, so far as the production of butadiene is concerned.
Except to buy petroleum?

We buy petroleum from the
plant in the first instance. Imperial Oil is in the business of selling petroleum and petroleum products. I can hardly imagine they would discriminate against the Polymer corporation, any more than they would discriminate against anyone else in Canada. I say they are in no preferred position, so far as any arrangement the government may make with the Polymer plant.

Has anyone
else a pipeline over there?

There are only two pipelines into Canada, so far as that goes. There is the pipeline from Portland to Montreal, and to Sarnia from the mid-continent fields of the United States. Those two pipelines come into Canada. But if Imperial Oil refused to sell to Polymer, we could certainly buy petroleum from other sources.
My hon. friend has a very curious idea of business in Canada, if he thinks that one of our big corporations would refuse to sell to one and would sell to another. That process is 100-1201
unthinkable. Therefore I think we can say that Imperial Oil have no proprietary interests in any way in the Polymer plant.
The second question was as to how rubber has been distributed among the manufacturers. Every rubber company I know of, either large or small, has been and is operating at full capacity. And every rubber company I know of in Canada that is manufacturing war goods has been supplied with all the raw material it can convert. The actual distribution of rubber, both the importing of rubber, the stock-piling of it, and the marketing of buna-S rubber, has been handled by a government corporation known as Fairmont Company Limited, which has been responsible for that operation since the period of a scarcity of rubber began. I believe it has handled that situation with great success.
That is mostly natural rubber that they are distributing.

In the early days. To-day they are using almost entirely synthetic rubber. There is a small stock-pile of natural rubber which is being very carefully guarded for such uses as may require natural rather than synthetic rubber.
Has the minister any information with respect to synthetic-rubber, since it came into production?

It has been distributed in Canada. Everyone in Canada has all he can use, all that the capacity of his plant will permit him to use. We never have had a period at any time when we have not been able to supply all the raw rubber required for war needs-and of course I am speaking only of war needs; not peace-time needs-that our plants could fabricate.
With reference to the question in connection with grain alcohol, I may say that I discussed that matter thoroughly the other day. If my hon. friend can tell me how to get more than two gallons of alcohol out of a bushel of wheat, then he will have an argument. But until then, I do not think he has any real argument.
Has the minister any information as to why they are using it in the United States?

They are using it because it can be brought in much more quickly than-the butadiene made from petroleum. They have been using it, just as we have been using it, because the butadiene base of petroleum was not available. It is available here now. It is becoming available in the United States,, and there will be a changeover.
Progress reported.

Mr. Speaker, last Monday night at *eleven o'clock I was speaking in the debate -on the motion to go into supply, and was [DOT]dealing with a matter of concern to many people. I had hoped that when I had an *opportunity to conclude my remarks I would be able to persuade the government that it should meet the request I was making.
I rise to-night to express pleasure that my speech has been taken away from me, by the announcement made at three o'clock this afternoon by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson). As hon. members will recall, the point I made last Monday night was that something should be done about the heavy burden facing people in connection with paying the balance of their income tax which would fall due on April 30. I am sure the country generally will be pleased with the decision finally made by the government in this matter, as announced this afternoon by the minister. I wish to express my pleasure that the government saw fit, in connection with this postponement of the final date, to provide that no interest will be chargeable on the balance due.
While I am on my feet I should like to refer to another matter which comes under the heading of the payment of last year's income tax. I shall not take much time, because the matter has been discussed before on two or three occasions. I earnestly hope the department of government responsible will see to it that an announcement is made soon with respect to the income tax status of the men of the 13th Canadian infantry brigade who went to Kiska last year. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), who for the moment, is also acting Minister of Finance, perhaps might confer with himself in the matter. He has stated on two or three occasions that an announcement would be made shortly. I would point out to the minister and the government that the men affected, as are other taxpayers, are wrestling with the making out of their returns. Those returns must be completed and filed by the end of April, even though payment may be deferred. I would hope that the announcement we have been looking for might be made at an early date.
It will be noticed that I am not arguing the case to-night. I am going so far as to assume

that when the announcement is made it will be favourable, and that the government will decide that these men are to be considered as having gone outside the western hemisphere so far as income taxes are concerned. I earnestly hope that such an announcement will be made before the house rises at the end of the week and that the men who served at Kiska will be told that they do not have to pay income tax for the period during which they were engaged on that expedition.

Mr. Speaker, within the next month the farmers of Canada, particularly those of western Canada, will be on the land. It is needless to say that this would be a most opportune time to have a clear statement made by the government with reference to its agricultural marketing policy for 1944. The year which has just passed, 1943, showed a slight falling off in acreage and a material drop in the amount of cereal crops produced in Canada. I should like to direct attention to some figures which appeared in the dominion bureau of statistics crop report issued on January 21, 1944, as follows:

Not in marketing.

As I say, part of this was owing to the greatly reduced per unit production, but it was also in part on account of the reduced acreage.

There was a drop of nearly one half million acres cultivated to field crops. Despite the fact that the value of cereal grains per bushel has greatly increased over last year, the aggregate return to the farmer is down slightly owing to the greatly reduced production. The total gross farm value of all field crops produced was $1,179,073,000 in 1942 as compared with $1,104,065,000 in 1943. It is interesting

The Economic Annalist issued by the Department of Agriculture shows that the index commodity figure for animal products is slightly above parity, while the index commodity figure for field products is still considerably below parity. The field products index commodity figure is 91-7, taking 1926 as the base of 100, whereas the farm cost of living, with a 1935-39 base of 100, is 121-9. The index commodity figure for all farm produce, including animal products which is 126-1, is still only 104-6, which is still somewhat below parity for the price which is paid to the farm population of the Dominion of Canada. Therefore, I desire to move, seconded by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright):
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"This house desires to record its opinion that the agricultural marketing policy of the government is detrimental to the public interest, and that steps should be taken to bring it into conformity with the needs of the farming population."
In the few moments I have at my disposal to-night I wish to outline some of the steps which we in this group think should be taken to bring the government's agricultural marketing policy in line with the needs of the farming population of Canada. I am going to confine myself to dealing with grain crops, letting some of my colleagues deal with other aspects of agriculture. I should like to suggest five steps which I think should be taken with reference to the marketing of cereal crops.
The first has to do with grain deliveries. Almost all western members will remember that last fall the farmers living on branch lines experienced great difficulty in delivering their crop. Parts of my constituency off the main line were as late as the first week in December. At that time many of them had been able to deliver less than five bushels per acre of their basic crop. I wired the wheat board and they explained that they were taking most of the wheat off the main line because they had to get it to the head of the lakes before the shipping season was closed. One could not argue against that, but it still did not help the people on the branch lines who had wheat in their granaries or piled in their back yards and were not able to dispose of it while their obligations were piling up at
Agricultural Marketing Policy
the stores, to their doctors, in the form of taxes to the municipalities and in the way of threshing bills.
The problem of financing has been quite serious, especially in the grain districts. Where farmers were doing a fair percentage of mixed farming they were able to dispose of some of their live stock in order to pay their threshing bills and meet other obligations. They were thus able to wait until such time as they could deliver their grain. But in other districts the farmers were principally grain farmers. In the southern part of the province and in some parts of my constituency the farmers are almost exclusively wheat farmers. In the northern part of the province, in the constituency of the hon. member for Melfort where they produce large quantities of coarse grains, the fact that they could not dispose of these coarse grains or their wheat meant that they had all the expense of taking off the crop and no ready cash with which to meet their many obligations. To deal with that situation we suggest that two things should be done; first, that the government should still give some consideration to a policy which has been followed with success in the United States, of giving the farmer a cash advance for wheat stored on the farm; second, that the government should pay storage, as they did once before, of the same amount per bushel which is paid to line elevator companies, for storing wheat and coarse grains on the farm.
I remember, in the year when the government did pay storage, a very successful farmer in my constituency built a large granary, with a cement floor, a cement wall rising three or four feet around it, a fine frame top and shingled roof. He built it with the idea that he would be able to store his wheat throughout the war period and that, if he were not able to deliver it, at least he could keep it on his farm and, if he stored the wheat over a period of years, the storage charges, which the government were then paying, would make a substantial contribution towards paying the cost of putting up that granary. What happened? The government discontinued the storage payments, and the result is that this man is to-day storing wheat in a first-class granary which is just as safe and just as well kept as if it were in the line elevator two miles down the road; but the difference is that for the wheat in the line elevator the company is drawing two-thirds of a cent per month, or eight cents a year, storage charges from the government of Canada, and the man who built this granary, and has served the country just as well by storing the wheat for the country's convenience, finds he gets no storage payment whatsoever.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to rise to a point of order. I have just got for the first time a copy of the hon. gentleman's amendment. It reads as follows:
This house desires to record its opinion that the agricultural marketing policy of the government is detrimental to the public interest, and that steps should be taken to bring it into conformity with the needs of the farming population.
I direct Your Honour's attention to page five of the estimates, items 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, and specifically, 28, "marketing of agricultural products, including temporary appointments that may be required to be made. ..." I suggest that, in consonance with a previous ruling of Your Honour during this session, this amendment is out of order.

Before Your Honour gives a ruling, may I point out, first of all, that this amendment is almost word for word identical with a motion I moved last year, on March 30, 1943, which was also challenged and which was accepted by Your Honour. May I point out in the second place that there is no single estimate which covers the whole field of the government's agricultural marketing policy. If the interpretation which the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie), is now attempting to place on that ruling were accepted, there is no question which by any stretch of the imagination could be discussed by any hon. member on a motion to go into supply.

Following the statement made by the hon. member, we have had an illustration to-night from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) of an item which can be discussed on a motion for going into supply. I can recall many other items of the kind. I have already given a ruling with regard to motions which can be and will be brought up in the house for discussion; and when it is pointed out to me that in the estimates, page five, Nos. 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, and 27 all deal with agriculture and marketing service, and especially No. 28, "marketing of agricultural products, including temporary appointments that may be required to be made, notwithstanding anything contained in the Civil Service Act, the amount available for such appointments not to exceed $15,000", I find that the amendment which is proposed: "This house desires to record its opinion that the agricultural marketing policy . . ." are exactly the words used in the item I have just quoted, and fall within the [DOT]category of those amendments which I have
(Mr. T. C. Douglas.]
already ruled out of order on the motion that the house go into committee of supply. I therefore must rule this amendment out of order.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that I believe such a ruling will so greatly restrict private members in this house as to make it impossible for them to express any opinion they have, I must regretfully appeal from your decision.
And five hon. members having risen:
Mr. SPEAKER put the question as follows:
The question is that I do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of supply, to which Mr. Douglas (Weyburn) moves in amendment:
"That all the words after 'that' be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"This house desires to record its opinion that the agricultural marketing policy of the government is detrimental to the public interest, and that steps should be taken to bring it into conformity with the needs of the farming population."
I have ruled the amendment out of order on the ground that it falls within the main estimates under items 22 to 28 inclusive, which will be subjects for discussion when these items are before the house.
